**Reading.** Fix C does what its sources say: initiations at Crameri's newly destructive rate per
km of subduction zone, at their distances, and its new plates live (dead within 20 Myr a third as
often). What it takes away is PLT-063's other role. The old rule recycled old floor far from every
trench by starting a subduction zone in it; Crameri find no such event, so old floor far from a
subduction zone now waits for a trench to reach it. In this model a trench reaches it only with
its plate: there is no rollback and no along-strike propagation (law 2 is parked). The floor ages,
fewer plates are born, and the plates merge into fewer, larger ones. These are findings, not
targets (V1 and the plate checks are realism checks, decisions log 2026-10-23); the lever is the
missing laws of a moving trench, not the rate.

**What it is not.** It places and paces newly destructive initiation only. It has no law for a
young subduction zone to propagate or roll back (law 2 is parked), none for the episodic jump with
transference off, and the polarity reversals stay the contacts' own. Crameri's transform faults
("Transform faults are also often present in the proximity of the SZI event location") are not
read: the reach is from subduction zones alone. The 150 Myr gate, the old rate and the 1,000 km
clearance hold with the switch off. The viewer's editor listed `subduction_start_rate`, `_age` and
`_clearance` (`crates/deeptime-viewer/assets/editor_fields.json`), which are inert with fix C on;
since 7d0506e3 (2026-10-26) it leaves them out, with the catalogue's comment saying why.

### Step 15: the moving trench, back-arc rifting and law 2 in Zhou's geometry (PLT-710 to PLT-717) (2026-10-26)

The M5 lane's stage 3, by the coordinator's order: the laws of a moving trench that Step 14 found
missing, trench rollback and along-strike propagation, diagnosed and sourced first, built behind
switches with unit tests against the sources, one cumulative arm and an off check (against
base24-s4: master moved to 3ce1a373, the collision belts' PLT-700, before the arm started, and
the branch merged it).

**The diagnosis.** A front is fixed in the plate that holds it: the overriding plate's samples on
the boundary are the trench. So every trench moves with its overriding plate, Heuret & Lallemand
2005's Vt = Vup + Vd with Vd always 0, and nothing in the model lets a trench move on its own. That
half is Earth's: Heuret & Lallemand find "spontaneous trench rollback related to slab pull is
negligible with respect to upper plate motion", and Vt follows the sign of Vup at three non-neutral
zones in four. The other half is missing: Earth's trenches roll back where the overriding plate
splits and a back-arc basin opens behind its forearc (Table 1 has 29 of its 158 two-degree
segments in class E3, back-arc spreading, opening at 2.8 to 142.1 mm/yr, median 34.8). In a model
of rigid plates that is a split: the forearc and arc become a microplate, which the slab's suction
can then pull seaward of the rest. The model forbids such plates twice over: nothing splits an
overriding plate at its arc, and PLT-091 absorbs any plate under 0.003 of the sphere (0.0377 sr) at
the next resampling, while Bird 2003's back-arc microplates are 0.0002 to 0.016 sr.

**Why law 2 was parked, and whether the reason holds.** Law 2 (along-strike propagation onto a
passive margin, PLT-656 to PLT-659, "Law 2" below) was parked on 2026-10-26 because it never
advanced: its starts fired where the trench meets the margin at 45 to 90°, where U moves along the
margin, so the convergence across it at the tip was 0 to 15 km a step against the 100 km an
advance needs. That reason holds on today's master for the same starts: the geometry is the
lattice's and the plates', and neither fix C nor the speed scale changes which way U moves at such
a junction. The front lane's note names the remedy, a start only in Zhou et al. 2020's geometry,
where the trench runs on along the margin; this stage builds it (PLT-717).

**Back-arc rifting** (`tectonics.backarc_rifting`, PLT-710, `rifting::maybe_rift_backarc`, after
the step's initiations). Sdrolias & Müller 2006 read the Cenozoic back-arc basins of eight
subduction systems against the floor's age and the plates' absolute motions: back-arc basins
"develop when the age of subducting normal oceanic lithosphere is greater than 55 million years";
"back-arc basin formation is always preceded by an absolute motion of the overriding plate away
from the subduction hinge"; "Once back-arc extension is established, it continues regardless of
overriding plate motion"; the locus is "commonly in between the remnant and active volcanic arc".
Karig 1971 (abstract): "Active extension is restricted to arc systems with earthquakes deeper than
about 350 km". So a subducting front (`subduction::Pull::subducting_fronts`, now with each front's
subducting sample and boundary normal) qualifies where the floor coming in is older than 55 Myr
(PLT-712), the plate holding the front moves away from it (its velocity along the normal below 0,
in the mantle's frame, the model's stand-in for Sdrolias's hotspot frame), the pair's slab is 350
km or longer (PLT-713: the slab's length stands for its depth, as the pull reads it) and no
back-arc sliver holds it. Sdrolias's third condition, an intermediate dip steeper than 30°, has no
counterpart: the model has no dip. Java-Sunda and the Aleutians met the age condition "with no
resultant back-arc extension", so the conditions open a hazard, not a certainty.

**How often** (PLT-711). Each pair of plates with a qualifying front draws once a step with
probability 1 − e^(−λ), λ = h × dt, and a draw takes the pair's whole qualifying front, so h is the
rate at which qualifying front converts. Heuret & Lallemand's Table 1 (tabulated from its text
layer, 158 of its 159 segments) has 70 segments with a slab of 55 Myr or older, 68 of them under an
upper plate moving landward, and 16 of those spreading (E3): f = 16 / 68. Sdrolias & Müller date
four Cenozoic basins: South Fiji 33 to 25 Ma, Parece Vela and Shikoku 30 to 15 Ma, the Japan Sea
30 to about 15 Ma, the West Philippine Basin about 55 to 30-33 Ma, a mean spreading life D of 15.4
Myr. A front that converts at h and spreads for D holds a spreading back-arc on h D / (1 + h D) of
its length, so h = f / ((1 − f) D) = 16 / (52 × 15.375) = 0.0200 per Myr, about one draw in 50
Myr for a pair that keeps qualifying. Test `the_backarc_hazard_gives_earth_s_spreading_share`.

**The split and the size rule** (PLT-714, PLT-715). A draw splits off the holding plate's samples
within `arc_distance_km` (PLT-042, 200 km) of the pair's qualifying fronts: the forearc and the arc,
where Taylor & Karner 1983 (abstract) find the arc rifting "on either side of the line of active
volcanoes (±50 km)", below the quick lattice's spacing. The largest connected strip is the sliver;
fewer than 32 samples on either side refuses the draw (`backarc_refused`). The sliver is a plate
with the parent's motion (rift_onset and plate_birth with `origin` "back_arc"), linked to the
parent so that a back-arc that does not open heals (PLT-272: under 5 mm/yr along the shared
boundary for 10 Myr), and PLT-534's inheritance hands it the contact and the slab. It is on
`PlateState::backarcs` while it holds a subducting front, and the burial at a resampling leaves a
plate on that list alone below PLT-091's size: Bird 2003's back-arc microplates (Mariana 0.01037
sr, Tonga 0.00625, South Sandwich 0.00317, Manus 0.00020) are all but one below PLT-091's 0.0377
sr. Tests `a_backarc_rifts_over_an_old_deep_slab_behind_a_retreating_upper_plate` (the split, its
reach, the contact, the slab, the events and the list; each gate alone; off, not a draw of the
generator) and `a_sliver_holding_its_front_outlives_the_plate_size_rule`.

**What moves the sliver.** Nothing new. The sliver holds the front, so the force balance's suction
(PLT-186, PLT-540: a share of the pull and a mantle link along the trench's normal) acts on it and
no longer on the parent; the slab's own pull and resistance stay on the subducting plate. Lallemand
et al. 2008's anchoring (eq. 11, F_a = 6.6 η_m V_t sin α) would slow it; the model has no such term
for any plate and this stage adds none. Test `a_backarc_sliver_opens_at_earth_s_rates`
(`plates/tests.rs`): FRC-016's reference plate on the 40,000-sample lattice (a 3,000 km trench of a
full-length 80 Myr slab) with the overriding plate's forearc and arc split off (69 samples, 32 on
the front), through the force balance at the defaults: the back-arc opens at 75.5 mm/yr, inside
Table 1's E3 range (2.8 to 142.1) and about twice its median (34.8); the trench, which moved 9.3
mm/yr seaward with its plate before, rolls back at 77.3, under Schellart et al. 2007's fastest (6
to 16 cm/yr "only observed close to slab edges"). A free sliver is fast because the suction's
mantle link (0.3 × the slab's resistance) and the boundary links are all that hold it; Lallemand et
al.'s eq. 11 at their η_m of 10^20 Pa s (Table 4) would add a mantle link of about 5.6 × 10^20 N s
m^-2 per metre of trench and slow a free sliver by about a sixth (the agent's estimate, not built).

**Law 2 in Zhou's geometry** (PLT-717, `tectonics.margin_propagation`, on with this stage). A
start now needs the trench to run on along the margin: U's trench samples within 4 spacings of the
trench sample and U's coast floor within 2 spacings of the stretch's end must each read as a line
(PLT-659's rule), their strikes within atan(1.5 / 4) = 20.6° of each other (a border's offset,
PLT-534, over the trench's window), the trench sample within the border of the margin's line, and
the continent at least a plate's worth of samples (`min_samples`, 300 on the pool's lattice), which
drops arm fl-law2's "continents" of 1 to 11 samples. The rest of law 2 (the force test, the tear,
the advance, PLT-658's strength) is unchanged, and law 3 stays off. A first form of the gate, every
trench sample within 1.5 spacings of the margin's line, let a 45° junction through on the test
lattice; the strikes' angle does not (42° there, 0.6° where the trench runs on). Test
`a_trench_meeting_the_margin_at_an_angle_starts_nothing`; law 2's five tests in Zhou's geometry
pass unchanged.

**The measures** (PLT-716, written only with back-arc rifting on). Over the step's subducting
fronts, one spacing each: the trench's velocity along the normal (the holding plate's, seaward
positive), the convergence, the length retreating and the length within ±50 mm/yr, the length the
slivers hold and the length that qualifies, and the slivers' opening against their parents. Earth's
numbers: Heuret & Lallemand's table, Vt mean 8.5 mm/yr, retreat 0.484 of the segments, 0.917 within
±50, E3 0.184; Schellart et al. 2007's 244 segments, mean vT 15.1 mm/yr and "27.6% of the total
subduction rate is due to trench migration".

**The arm** (trench3c: both laws on by default, key c6e9fcafc97b, argkey cd665cef, `pool.sh run
trench3c --seeds 1,2,3,4` with the crust-budget envs; against base24-s4, base24's cached seeds 1 to
4 on master 3ce1a373; `pool.sh table` for guard and v1census, `build/m4b/s3_read.py` for the
records). Medians of 8 runs against 8, two-sided Mann-Whitney p in brackets.

- **Guard clean.** No step beyond 2 Earth reliefs in any run; the worst 10,471 m (base 10,172,
  p 0.13); the highest plate elevation 5,963 m (5,688).
- **V1.** Collisions 3.40 to 4.20 per 100 Myr (p 0.035), the only number at p < 0.05. Land 0.316 to
  0.289 (0.38), largest landmass 0.168 to 0.131 (0.96), continental crust under the sea 0.211 to
  0.252 (0.72), land above 2 km 0.059 to 0.030 (1.0), coast with high ground 0.109 to 0.124
  (0.88), land under ice 0.117 to 0.097 (0.88), crust's net change −0.065 to −0.071 (0.96);
  criteria met 5.5 to 6 (mean 5.50 to 5.38).
- **Back-arcs.** 49.5 back-arc rifts a run, 43 more drawn and refused (a sliver or a rest under 32
  samples: short qualifying fronts on the quick lattice); 3.5 alive at the end. They do open: none
  healed, and the slivers' opening against their parents averages 43.7 mm/yr over the fronts they
  hold (Heuret & Lallemand's E3 median 34.8, range 2.8 to 142.1). Their median life is 34.5 Myr
  (Sdrolias & Müller's four basins spread for 8 to 25 Myr); 31.5 of them end absorbed (PLT-091
  once they hold no subducting front), 8.5 sutured, 6 consumed. They hold 0.075 of the subducting
  front over the run (Heuret & Lallemand's E3 segments 0.184), and 0.107 qualifies unheld.
- **The trench's motion** (with the slivers in it). Mean Vt 15.6 mm/yr seaward (Schellart et al.
  2007 15.1 in the Indo-Atlantic hotspot frame; Heuret & Lallemand's table 8.5 in HS3), retreating
  on 0.743 of the front (Schellart 2008's 62 to 78 % of segments by frame; Heuret & Lallemand 0.484),
  0.895 within ±50 mm/yr (0.917), and trench migration 0.234 of the subduction rate (Schellart et
  al. 2007's 27.6 %; mean convergence 67.1 mm/yr). No base number exists: off, the measures are not
  written (they would break the off check), and every trench moves with its overriding plate.
- **Law 2.** 2.5 starts a run and 2.5 advances (arm fl-law2: 116 starts, none advanced), 15.5
  stalls; the margin broken about 390 km a run Earth-normalized (48 km of the quick planet's), at
  about 36 mm/yr while live (Zhou et al.'s model about 17 cm/yr); 2.5 new plates a run, median life
  110 Myr.
- **The plates.** Alive 12 to 15 (p 0.026), plate life 72 to 54.5 Myr (0.006), births 102 to 154.5
  (0.002), slab breakoffs 8.85 to 10.55 per 100 Myr (0.004), sutures 34 to 42 (0.030), partings
  11.7 to 14.3 per 100 Myr (0.040); the slab-attached plates' speed over the free ones 2.97 to 2.47
  (0.010), the slab pull's share of the drive 0.665 to 0.514 (0.021): the slivers are small plates
  whose drive is the suction, not a slab of their own.
- **The floor**, Step 14's open question: median age 94.5 to 90.7 Myr (0.51), older than 180 Myr
  23.2 to 22.0 % (0.51), older than 250 Myr 13.0 to 12.3 % (0.51). The moving trench does not
  reach the old floor: it sits beside the continents, far from any trench (the age map, "The sea
  floor's age" below), and law 2's few propagations take little of it.

**The off check.** Both switches off (trench3c-off, `--set tectonics.backarc_rifting=false --set tectonics.margin_propagation=false`, key c6e9fcafc97b, argkey a3bb8920, seed 1 of both starts): base24's planet bit for bit, the world state's 109 and 108 files, the dumped fields and the dynamics record sha256 for sha256 (`build/m4b/offcheck_s3.sh`); only the parameter dump, the two new counters' names and the timings differ.

**What it is not.** The sliver's speed comes from the model's suction and boundary terms alone:
there is no slab-width law (Schellart et al. 2007: retreat "inversely related to slab width",
fastest within 1,200 km of a slab edge), no anchoring (Lallemand et al. 2008), no dip, and no
mantle flow or plume under the back-arc. A draw takes a pair's whole qualifying front, where
Earth's back-arcs open along segments of a long trench. A back-arc's spreading does not end by a
law of its own (Sdrolias & Müller: "The cessation of back-arc spreading cannot be correlated with
any surface kinematic events"); here it ends when the sliver stops opening (it heals), loses its
front (it is absorbed at a resampling) or collides. The trench-motion measures are written only
with back-arc rifting on. Law 2's tolerances are the lattice's (PLT-717, `game-choice`), and its
margin strength is still PLT-658's fallback.

### Step 16: the slab's thermal floor acts on a forming slab only (PLT-720) (2026-10-27)

The old-floor lane, then the coordinator (Ben paused the sub-agents on 2026-10-27). Step 14 and Step 15 left the floor
old (base25: median 90.7 Myr, older than 250 Myr 12.2 % on seeds 1 to 4; Earth 0.06 %, CHK-034). The lane's diagnosis
(tools/review/oldfloor/: oldfloor.py and oldfloor_read.py over the crust-budget maps, plateseries.py over rec.json)
found where much of it came from: planets that stalled. On base25 (24 runs) 5 runs had steps with under 2,000 km of
subduction front, 643 of 10,824 steps (5.9 %), and those steps held 0.238 of the summed share of floor older than
250 Myr; scattered_continents-3 had no subduction front from -600 to -50 Myr while 8 to 16 plates moved at 1.5 to
6.5 mm/yr with 12 or more slabs of 184 to 700 km and no pull on any plate (rec.json `forces`). Base18 to base22, before
fix C, had none such.

**Why they stalled.** PLT-681 (the slab's thermal floor) made any oceanic front sample converging under 10 mm/yr
incipient: no pull, no suction, no slab resistance, the incipient resistance instead. A collision that slowed the
large plates took every slab's pull away at once, and with fix C (PLT-690, no initiation without an active trench) no
new subduction zone could start, so the planet stayed still. Toth & Gurnis 1998's floor is narrower than that: "at
subduction velocities of <10 mm/yr thermal diffusion inhibits slab formation and no substantial slab pull force
develops" (p. 18,063), a test of whether a new subduction zone on a preexisting fault has formed within 20 Myr
(their title: "Dynamics of subduction initiation at preexisting fault zones"). A slab that has formed keeps its
negative buoyancy whatever its plate's speed this step.

**The rule** (`tectonics.slab_floor_forming_only`, PLT-720, on by default). In the force balance the floor holds an
oceanic front sample only while its contact's slab is forming (at PLT-610's incipient stage); a mature slab keeps its
pull, suction and slab resistance and the trench's Forsyth & Uyeda friction at any convergence, and takes no incipient
resistance (`forces::floor_holds_in_balance`). The arcs, the boundary mix, the margins and fix C's active trenches
still read PLT-681 per sample. Test: `a_formed_slab_pulls_under_the_thermal_floor` (the reference plate with a full
slab pushed at 5 mm/yr, the floor on: with the switch its slab pulls).

**The arm** (oldfloor720, key ff5d8ceda63e, argkey cd665cef, seeds 1 to 4 of both starts, against base25-s4; medians,
two-sided Mann-Whitney p in brackets):
- the guard: clean, worst 10,471 to 10,253 m (0.51), no step beyond two Earth reliefs;
- the floor (the plate check): median age 90.7 to 81.1 Myr, older than 180 Myr 22.0 to 19.1 %, older than 250 Myr
  12.2 to 10.1 %; plate life 54.5 to 47.0 Myr; plates alive 15 to 16; continental minimum 0.340 to 0.339;
- V1: nothing at p < 0.05; land 0.289 to 0.316, largest landmass 0.131 to 0.163, crust under the sea 0.252 to 0.192,
  land above 2 km 0.030 to 0.056, ice 0.097 to 0.060, collisions 4.20 to 4.15, crust net -0.071 to -0.072, criteria 6
  in both; coast with high ground 0.124 to 0.215 (0.33), up on 6 of the 8 seeds run by run (a finding for the coast
  work, not a target here: moving plates keep more active margins).

**The off check** (oldfloor720-off, `--set tectonics.slab_floor_forming_only=false`, argkey 100da219, seed 1 of both
starts): base25's planet bit for bit, the world state, the record and the fields equal by sha256.

**What it is not.** The floor still ages: floor older than 250 Myr stays near 10 %, against Earth's trace. The rest of
it sits beside the continents, far from any trench, which no law here reaches; trench invasion of an Atlantic-type
ocean (Duarte et al. 2013) and induced initiation at a passive margin (Stern & Gerya 2018) are the lane's candidates,
not built.

### Step 17: transference on by default (PLT-516) (2026-10-27)

The coordinator, inline (no lane runs while Ben has the sub-agents paused). Step 16 left about a tenth of the
floor older than 250 Myr, most of it beside continents far from any trench. With fix C (PLT-690) a subduction zone
starts only within 1,500 km of an active one, so where a collision chokes an ocean's last trench nothing new
starts there, and base26 counts no transference in any of its 26 runs (the switch was off). The sources read for
the old floor agree on what closes such an ocean: Stern 2004's transference ("the oceanic lithosphere outboard of
the collision zone ultimately ruptures to become a new subduction zone"), Crameri et al. 2020's episodic subduction
(5 of their 13 events since 104 Ma: "an arc is accreted to the overriding plate and subduction jumps to the front";
"collisional events along a pre-existing subduction trench ... temporally and spatially coincide with SZI events"),
and Duarte et al. 2018 ("the only source to provide a force conceivably capable of inducing subduction initiation
along a pristine passive margin is another subduction system or an associated collision belt"). PLT-516 is that
law, built by the docking lane on 2026-10-23 and held off then because the plate check failed under it (the
continental share's highest, the arcs' continental heights, the largest land gain) before the model had a sink
of continental area; it has one now (PLT-660's sediment subduction among them: base26-s4's continents lose 7.2 %
of their crust over a run).

**The call** (the coordinator's, undoable): on by default. It is a verified law from Stern 2004 and Crameri et al.
2020, not a knob; it moves no V1 measure out of its target and moves the one that was out (the coast with high
ground) toward it; the floor goes the way Earth's does. With the switch off the planet is base26's
(`--set tectonics.transference=false`). A 24-run base follows on the merged master.

**What it is not.** The floor older than 250 Myr stays near 7 %, against the check's 3 % and Earth's trace: the

is the next candidate.

### Step 18: where the old floor sits after transference (diagnosis, 2026-10-27)

The coordinator, inline, on base27 (master f4662d49, transference on; 24 runs, seeds 1 to 4 read here). Floor older
than 250 Myr is 5.9 % of the ocean (the plate check's median; 3 % its line, Earth's present trace). The research for
the next law (trench invasion: Duarte et al. 2013, 2024; Waldron et al. 2014; Schellart et al. 2007, 2008; Pindell &
Kennan 2009; bibliography notes of 2026-10-27) expected Atlantic-type oceans, open floor trailing a continent far from
any trench, which a trench entering through a corridor would consume. The diagnosis does not find that.

- **The plates that hold it** (tools/review/oldfloor/oldfloor_plates.py, every snapshot from -900 Myr): 55 % of it on
  plates over 0.2 of the planet, 72 % on plates moving 20 mm/yr or more, 67 % on plates that go down at 5,000 km or
  more of slab front, 80 % on plates a quarter or more continental; only 10 % on slow plates (under 20 mm/yr) with
  under 2,000 km of front. The plates are working, not stalled.
- **Which side of its continent**: on the great circle to its own plate's nearest trench, 53 % meets its own
  continent first ("trails"), 42 % does not ("leads"), 4 % is on plates with no trench. Of the trailing floor 80 % is
  more than 1,500 km from any subduction front and 87 % from any collision front; of the leading floor 50 % is within
  1,500 km of a subduction front (fix C's reach) and still old. (Corrected after Graphide's review of PR #14: the side
  and distance tables had been divided by the plate tables' count, which leaves out plates missing from the record's
  step; first read 55, 39, 5, 81, 86 and 55 %.)
- **Enclosure** (tools/review/oldfloor/oldfloor_enclosed.py): of 16 directions from each old sample, the share that
  meets continental crust within 2,000 km: 12 or more for 63 % of the old floor, all 16 for 23 %, mostly its own
  plate's continent (12 or more: 53 %). The map of the worst run (tools/review/oldfloor/agemap.py: supercontinent-2,
  t0000, 13,628 of 66,782 ocean samples older than 250 Myr) shows it: basins ringed by continents inside the
  assembled continental masses, some joined to the open ocean only by a young rift, and floor near the north pole.
- **Not the collisions' length**: base27's collisions last 40 Myr at the median (the plate check's 15 to 50), keep
  0.46 of their onset convergence after 20 Myr (0.2 to 0.6) and shorten 913 km at the median, 2,060 km at the 90th
  percentile (India-Asia about 2,000 to 3,000), so plates do not weld early across open basins on the whole.
- **The passive margins** (oldfloor.py): mean standing age 181 Myr on base26, 154 on base27; older than 250 Myr 27 %
  and 20 % of the margin snapshots, against Bradley 2008's 11 % of margin-time (Phanerozoic starts: mean 79 Myr, none
  older than 220).

Earth keeps enclosed oceanic basins too, and they hold its oldest floor (the Eastern Mediterranean's, about 340 Myr,
Granot 2016), but they are small. So the next law is about how the model's basins become enclosed and what closes
them, not about invasion alone: where the floor enclosed by one plate's continents came from (welds across a basin,
healed rifts, arcs turned continental round a basin, PLT-668), and the closure Duarte et al. 2013 name for a passive
margin, a force "transmitted from a nearby subduction zone or collisional belt" (fix C counts subduction zones only).
Candidates, none built: initiation within reach of active collision fronts as of subduction zones; a tear between a
pair's collided and still-subducting stretches (Govers & Wortel 2005's STEP, as law 2 uses), so a collision does not
stop a whole rigid boundary; trench invasion with Schellart et al.'s slab-width rule for rollback.

**The first candidate is dropped, and the welds are measured** (the coordinator, 2026-10-27, after PR #14). A Sonnet
research sub-agent read Crameri et al. 2020's Table 1 and Supplementary Notes 1 to 13: collision is the trigger, or
the likely one, of 6 of the 13 initiations (the Olutorsky arc at the Aleutians, Palawan at the Philippine trench, the
Ontong Java plateau at New Hebrides-New Britain, Papuan blocks at Tonga-Kermadec, Siletzia at Cascadia, the Gagua
Ridge at the Ryukyus), all arcs, plateaus, ridges or microcontinents arriving at a trench that was already there, none a
continental collision belt, and all within 1,500 km of active subduction. Four of the six are Table 1's polarity
reversals (Aleutian, Philippine, New Hebrides-New Britain, Tonga-Kermadec) and two its episodic jumps of a trench to
the front of what docked (Cascadia, Ryukyu). Fix C's rate (PLT-692) counts none of them (only the four newly
destructive initiations); the model has them elsewhere, at the jammed trench itself: the reversal (PLT-371) and the
docked terrane's transfer to the overriding plate (PLT-068, and PLT-516's transference for a continent), after which the
force balance decides what the new boundary does. So the six are no evidence for new trenches starting near a collision
belt, which is what the candidate would add (corrected after Graphide's review of PR #15: the first draft said fix C
would count them twice). Duarte et al. 2013's "nearby subduction zone or collisional belt" stays the setting of one
margin (South-West Iberia, where the Gibraltar arc is a subduction zone), not a rate. Stern & Gerya 2021 (Encyclopedia of Geology, read in full) define transference as the
"trench jump" after an arc or plateau docks and write "There are no Cenozoic examples of SI by transference": India
went on colliding rather than start a trench in the Indian Ocean. base27 transfers 14.2 continents per 1,000 Myr (the
24 runs' mean, 29 % of its 49 collisions), 0.94 expected in the Cenozoic's 66 Myr, so none there has a chance of 0.39
(PLT-516's row).

The welds (tools/review/oldfloor/oldfloor_welds.py, base27's 24 runs): a run welds 33 plates (median), the plate that
goes holds 2.9 % of the planet at the median and 11.9 % at the 90th percentile, and 54 % of it is ocean floor; the
floor taken into other plates sums to 0.94 of the planet's area over a run (0.63 to 1.18), and 112 of the 838 welds
take a plate of a tenth of the planet or more. That floor keeps its age and loses its plate's boundary with the
continents it has just met, which fits Step 18's map, floor ringed by one plate's continents. PLT-246's weld is a
`game-choice` (5 mm/yr for 10 Myr, no source for either), so the next step is the weld itself: whether a plate with
open floor left between it and the other plate should become one with it, against Earth's record of plates that
stopped converging (India has not, after 50 Myr), before any new hazard.

### Step 19: the weld is the old floor's trap; the stall needs the plates to stop moving (2026-10-27)

The coordinator, inline, after Step 18 found the floor older than 250 Myr in basins ringed by one plate's continents
and base27's welds taking 0.94 of the planet's area of ocean floor into other plates per run.

- **Two diagnostic arms** (the pool, master's key ecc431ae09c1, earthlike_quick_16k, 1000 Myr, seeds 1 to 4 from both
  starts, 8 runs each, read against base27's same 8 runs, medians): with no weld at all (`--set
  tectonics.weld_after_myr=100000`, arm weld-off) the floor older than 250 Myr falls from 6.9 % to 2.6 % of the ocean,
  older than 180 Myr from 15.5 % to 7.9 %, the floor's 90th-percentile age from 276 to 170 Myr (Earth's oldest floor in
  place is about 180 Myr) and its median from 75 to 59 Myr; the steps with one plate over half the planet from 13.6 % to
  none, the largest plate's median share from 0.31 to 0.21, the plates alive from 17 to 26. With the weld speed at 1
  mm/yr instead of 5 (arm weld1) the welds fall from 33.5 to 12.5 a run and the floor older than 250 Myr to 4.8 %. So
  the weld is what keeps the old floor: a plate welded with its ocean floor keeps that floor inside a plate ringed by
  continents, with no trench, until the supercontinent breaks.
- **What Earth does** (research sub-agent, 2026-10-27, bibliography notes): reconstructions merge plates mostly when a
  ridge between them dies (India and Australia at 43 Ma, Seton et al. 2012, Morra et al. 2013), rarely after a
  collision (Iberia captured by Eurasia at 28 Ma, Seton et al. 2012); collisions go on converging for a long time
  (India-Asia still 40 to 50 mm/yr after 50 Myr, van Hinsbergen et al. 2011; Africa-Eurasia 4.5 to 5.5 mm/yr about 80
  Myr after its onset, and still a plate boundary); the ocean trapped when plates stop is small (the Herodotus Basin
  about 0.13 million km², the Levantine Sea 0.32, the Black Sea 0.44) against the welded plates' median 8 million km² of
  ocean in base27.
- **Two faults in the weld rule** (PLT-246): its speed, 5 mm/yr, had no source, and Earth keeps Africa and Eurasia apart
  at that speed; Bird 2003 (paragraph [3], the source library's copy read) overlooks "internal velocity variations of
  as much as 2 to 8 mm/a; the lower threshholds apply in regions of slow relative plate motion (e.g., North America,
  Atlantic Ocean, Mediterranean, Africa)", so plates moving apart by less than 2 mm/yr in a slow region are one plate
  and those by more are two. And the stall read the convergence across the front alone, so two plates whose collision
  turned to strike-slip welded while sliding past each other; the rule's own design ("two plates are one plate when they
  have stopped moving relative to each other", force-balance design 3.4) and Bird's velocity variations are motion in
  any direction.
- **The law** (`tectonics.weld_on_relative_speed`, on by default, PLT-721; `weld_speed_mm_yr` 2, PLT-246): a collision
  stalls when both its convergence across the front and the plates' relative speed along the front (Σ edge length ×
  relative speed over the edge length, `Front::relative_speed_mm_yr`) stay under 2 mm/yr for `weld_after_myr`.

**Sources for that step, and base29's numbers** (2026-10-29, the coordinator; a Sonnet research sub-agent read Lallemand &
Arcay 2021 in full and Stern & Scholl 2010's pp. 16 and 18, bibliography `LallemandArcay2021`, `SternScholl2010`). The boundary measure's `front_coll_km` is a run's mean
(`plates/collision_front_km_myr` over the run), and Stern & Scholl 2010 (p. 16) give ~12,000 km of active suture today,
an average of ~6,000 km over the supercontinent cycle (after Scholl & von Huene 2009) and 1,000 to 20,000 km over
geologic time; so base29's 13,356 km is about 2.2 times Earth's mean, not 1.1 times the registry's bound. Lallemand &
Arcay 2021 (70 Cenozoic initiations): a collision is the trigger of about half (p. 74), the new zone forms "either on
the opposite side of the upper plate volcanic arc (flip) or less frequently back of the lower plate buoyant feature
(jump or transference)" (p. 82), it takes "3 to ~15 Myr" to succeed (p. 86), and in their Melanesian cases the
collisions "shutdowned the previous SZs" (p. 83). Where a collision ends on Earth, then, is mostly a new subduction
zone taking over its convergence within about 15 Myr, which bears on the model's fronts that converge at 12 to 13
mm/yr for 60 Myr and more (Docking, above). base29 (`pool.sh table --base base28 --arm base29 --registry
tools/review/pool/measures_boundary.json --measure boundary`): the active share of the continental margin 0.444,
the coast at a subduction front 0.192 and in a collision belt 0.257, collision length p50 / p90 42 / 76 Myr,
polarity reversals 9.8 and initiations 4.15 per 100 Myr. The docking measures on the same runs (`pool.sh measure --arm
base29 --registry tools/review/pool/measures_docking.json --measures sutures,coastwalk`): 38.9 sutures and 37,944 km of
suture per 100 Myr (Macdonald et al. 2019: 19 to 39 and 23,235 to 50,919), a median suture of 427 km (his 1,019); at
a run's end 18,683 km of collision front open, 0.71 of it on contacts over 60 Myr old, the open collisions 33 Myr
along (median) at a median peak of 44.5 mm/yr; in the last 30 Myr 0.84 of the front-time is collisions that end
with no hand-off or are still open. The sutures are Earth's in number and length. At a run's end, then, the open
fronts sit mostly on old contacts; over the whole run they do not (the next paragraph: by a collision state's own
age, most of the front-time is collisions under 30 Myr old). One run, supercontinent seed 1, made 17 transferences
and 79 polarity reversals in 1000 Myr.

**Where the shortened crust goes** (2026-10-29, the coordinator; a second Sonnet research sub-agent, full texts,
bibliography `WillettBeaumontFullsack1993`, `NaylorSinclair2008`, `Simoes2007`, `Dahlen1990`). Over base29's 24 runs the
front-time by a collision state's age (the dock tally, after the first 100 Myr; medians) is 0.189 under 10 Myr (41.8
mm/yr), 0.387 at 10 to 30 Myr (29.5), 0.294 at 30 to 60 Myr (7.4) and 0.118 past 60 Myr (6.2): mostly young fronts
converging fast, not base3's old ones (the contacts can be old while the states on them are young: a contact
hands its collision on to a new state every 100 km of shortening, PLT-068). At the front of the youngest the overriding plate's edge is dry for 0.334 of the
front-time (10 to 30 Myr: 0.551). The wedge on the incoming plate rises only up to that edge's height
(`wedge_reach_km = (z_front - (sea - 500 m)) / tan(wedge_slope_deg)`, PLT-244), so against a submerged edge there is
little or no wedge and the belt on the overriding plate takes the crust, at what becomes the coast. Earth's orogens do
the reverse: a doubly vergent orogen keeps most of its mass in the pro-wedge over the lower plate (Naylor & Sinclair
2008, p. 21; about 62 % with their assumed 1.5 and 2.5 degree slopes, pp. 8-9), at an active margin "a large accretionary
wedge obeying pro-wedge mechanics and a smaller landward-verging retro-wedge ... overlying the arc basement" (Willett
et al. 1993, p. 373), and Taiwan's 90 km belt is the Chinese margin's crust with the Luzon arc as its backstop (Dahlen
1990, pp. 83-84; Simoes et al. 2007, p. 1). That is the lead for the coast with high ground; nothing is changed yet.

### Step 20: two wedges about the suture (PLT-730, PLT-731; 2026-10-29)

The coordinator, inline, from the lead above and the design `docs/design/collision-two-wedges.md`. A switch,
`tectonics.collision_two_wedges`, off by default when built (its pool arm below); **on by default since 2026-10-31**
(the coordinator's call, decisions log 2026-10-31; "The collision orogen (PLT-740)" below).

- **The rule.** A doubly vergent orogen grows as two critical wedges about the point S where the lower plate's mantle
  goes down: a pro-wedge over the lower plate at the minimum critical taper, a retro-wedge over the upper plate,
  steeper, at the maximum (Willett, Beaumont & Fullsack 1993, p. 372). With the switch the crest stands at the front.
  The pro-wedge's surface falls from it over the incoming plate at `wedge_slope_deg` (alpha, 1.5 degrees, PLT-192), the
  retro-wedge's over the overriding plate at beta, `retro_slope_ratio` (PLT-731) times as steep, both from one crest
  height H:
  S_pro(d) = min(H, h_s) - d tan alpha and S_retro(d) = min(h_s, H - d tan beta), with h_s the strength height
  (PLT-253). The step's crust raises the ground under both surfaces with H found by bisection so that all of it is
  placed (`fill_two_wedges`). On even ground each side takes its cross-section, H^2 / (2 tan), so the pro-wedge takes
  tan beta / (tan alpha + tan beta) of the crust (0.61 at the ratio 1.55; "more mass is stored in the pro-wedge
  than the retro-wedge", Naylor & Sinclair 2008, p. 21); a lower side takes more, so a drowned overriding edge fills
  before the crest rises over the incoming plate's lowland. Past the strength height the pro-wedge stops rising and the
  retro side widens as a plateau, as the taper belt does (Tibet behind the Himalaya, Dahlen 1990, p. 96). What both
  cannot hold at the strength height goes to the no-room rule (PLT-700) as before.
- **The retro slope** (PLT-731; a Sonnet research sub-agent, 2026-10-29, full texts, bibliography `DavisSuppeDahlen1983`,
  `WillettSlingerlandHovius2001`, `He2021`). No source read states a retro-wedge's regional slope in its text. The one
  orogen measured on both flanks is Taiwan: the western (pro) slope is 2.9 degrees (Davis, Suppe & Dahlen 1983, p.
  1163) and their section labels the eastern surface above the sea 4.5 degrees (Fig. 10, p. 1162, read with p. 1171),
  so tan beta / tan alpha = 1.55. The model's alpha is the Himalaya's 1.5 degrees, and the Himalaya has no retro-wedge
  to measure (Tibet stands behind it), so the retro side is set as Taiwan's ratio, `retro_slope_ratio` 1.55, beta 2.33
  degrees, and the pro-wedge takes 0.61 of the crust on even ground. Willett, Slingerland & Hovius 2001 find the
  retro-wedge "steeper and shorter than the matching prowedge" in the Southern Alps, Taiwan and the Olympics (p. 477);
  southern Taiwan's mean local slopes stand 1.43 times steeper on the retro flank (He et al. 2021).
- **What it replaces.** The wedge capped by the overriding edge's height (PLT-244, with its floor PLT-380) and the taper
  belt from that edge (PLT-600, PLT-601) while the switch is on. The pro-wedge's reach is the fall from a crest at the
  strength height down to 500 m under the sea, (h_s - (S - 500 m)) / tan alpha, about 214 km, whatever the overriding
  edge's height. Everything else stays: the stacking share (PLT-242), the crust that crosses whole (PLT-400: the
  pro-wedge's crust rides its plate to the front, crosses whole and is stacked again on both sides), the overriding
  plate's interior share (PLT-652), the foredeep read beyond the pro-wedge's toe.
- **Which front.** PLT-600 read the model's front as the Himalaya's Main Frontal Thrust, the toe of a wedge on the
  overriding side. With two wedges the front is S instead: the model's front is where the incoming plate's samples are
  consumed and its crust leaves the incoming plate, which is where the lower plate goes down, and the incoming plate's
  samples in front of it carry the pro-wedge as the lower plate carries the Lesser Himalaya to the suture. The crest
  at S is a simplification: models put the topographic maximum somewhat retro-ward of the subduction point (Naylor &
  Sinclair 2008, p. 15, after Willett et al. 1993).
- **At the model's resolution.** The quick planet's samples are about 71 km apart on the model sphere, so a 3 km crest's
  pro-wedge (115 km at 1.5 degrees) is one or two rows and its retro-wedge one; the unit fixture's 16,000 samples
  (about 180 km apart) make each wedge its front row.
- **On the pool: the lead is refuted, the switch stays off** (this was the 2026-10-29 reading, set aside on 2026-10-31:
  the switch is on by default, "The collision orogen (PLT-740)" below; arm tw-wedges, key cfdf228e0c4c, `--set
  tectonics.collision_two_wedges=true` and base29's crust-budget environment, earthlike_quick_16k, 1000 Myr, seeds 1 to
  4 from both starts, 8 runs against base29's 24, medians, Mann-Whitney p in brackets; the arm ran with the first
  draft's absolute retro slope, 2.5 degrees, a ratio of 1.67 against the default's 1.55). The mechanism works: the
  incoming plate's wedge holds 0.39 of the collisions' kept crust at the end (the crust budget's `kept_wedge` over
  `kept`, two runs read) against about 0.03 under the capped wedge, less than the even-ground 0.62 because drowned
  overriding edges, lower, take more. But the coast with high ground rises from 0.159 to 0.207 (0.078), the
  collision regime's land within 150 km of the sea from 0.289 to 0.372 of it, and that land's median distance to the
  sea falls from 270 to 212 km (0.094; `measures_boundary.json`, `collcoast`). A crest at the front between two
  drowned margins stands at the sea on both sides, as Taiwan does, where the old belt's toe left a strip of sea or
  lowland in front of its 2 km line. Land above 2 km 0.049 to 0.039 (0.75), land 0.330 to 0.310 (0.064), the largest
  landmass 0.193 to 0.153 (0.20), collisions per 100 Myr 2.75 to 2.35 (0.045), the boundary mix unchanged (`boundary`,
  every share within 0.003). The guard (`guard`, base29 measured too): no step beyond two Earth reliefs in either, the
  highest plate elevation 5,418 m against 5,554 (0.29). So the
  wedge's cap is not what puts collision belts at the coast. The model reads its front as PLT-600 does (the toe) with
  the switch off by default; the two wedges stay as a measured alternative. The next lead is in the collision measure
  itself: 0.437 of the collision high coast is a belt running along the coast, and small terranes (under 50 samples)
  hand off 30.4 times per 100 Myr, so the belts along coasts may be terranes accreted to a margin with the sea behind
  them (not yet measured).
- **Where the collision regime stands** (2026-10-29, after the arm; base29's crust-budget maps, the map 50 Myr before
  each run's end, 24 runs, medians; scratch scripts, nothing kept). The collision regime is every sample stamped with a
  collision orogeny in the last 30 Myr (`collision_orogeny_myr`, PLT-247's stamp at 5 m/Myr). Its samples stand a
  median 1,463 km from the nearest sample the boundary mix flags as a collision front's overriding side
  (`MAP_FRONT_COLLISION`); 0.133 of them lie within the belt's 400 km and 0.491 beyond 1,500 km. Stamps of the last two
  steps alone (half of them, about 3,100 samples) are as far: a median 1,387 km, 0.125 within 400 km. The flag marks
  only part of the open front (about 110 samples, some 7,800 km), so the distances overstate, but the code says the
  same: the overriding plate's share (PLT-652, `upper_plate`) spreads its crust over a strip that is every continental
  sample of that plate between the front's ends and behind it, with no limit on depth, and stamps a collision orogeny
  wherever it adds 10 m in a step. So the collision regime reaches across whole overriding plates, and the measure's
  "coast in a collision belt" (0.257 of the coast) counts that stamped interior, not belts at the coast. Whether the
  interior's slow thickening is an orogeny, and how far behind a front it reaches, were read next (a Sonnet research
  sub-agent, 2026-10-29; bibliography `Gordon1998`, `Calais2006`, `Calais2003`, `Hao2019`). The stamp's 5 m/Myr of
  rise is about 1.0e-9 per year of crustal strain on a 35.1 km column (Airy's factor 7.02, PLT-281): above the upper bound of stable plate interiors,
  4e-10 per year (Gordon 1998, p. 615), and below what GPS resolves as deforming in Asia, 3e-9 per year (Calais et al.
  2006, p. 5). India's collision deforms Asia as far as Lake Baikal, about 3,000 km from the Himalayan front (Hao et
  al. 2019), but not as a strip: about 60 % of the area strains as slowly as stable interiors, with rigid blocks
  (Tarim, south and north China, Sunda) inside the deforming zone, the strain significant only in the high belts (the
  Himalaya, Tibet, the Pamir-Tien Shan, the Altay, the Baikal rift), and 15 % of the convergence taken north of the
  Tien Shan (Calais et al. 2003). So the interior share's reach has the sources behind it and its stamp does not: a
  column thickening below 3e-9 per year is not resolvably deforming. Nothing is changed yet; the rule to build is in
  STATUS's Follow-ups.
- **The interior's stamp at a resolvable strain rate** (PLT-732, `tectonics.collision_upper_stamp_resolvable`, on by
  default since 2026-10-29). The interior share's crust lands where it did; a column is stamped as part of the
  collision orogeny only where the step's share thickens it at 3e-9 per year or more (210.6 m of crust, 30.0 m of rise,
  on a 35.1 km column over a 2 Myr step), as well as by PLT-247's 5 m/Myr. The arm up-stamp (`--set
  tectonics.collision_upper_stamp_resolvable=true`, base29's environment, seeds 1 to 4 from both starts, 8 runs against
  base29's 24): the collision regime falls from 0.148 to 0.117 of the land, its fresh stamps (the last two steps,
  base29's crust-budget maps 50 Myr before the end) from about 3,100 samples a median 1,387 km from a flagged front to
  about 1,800 a median 820 km (0.24 within 400 km). The V1 checks do not move: coast with high ground 0.164 (0.92),
  land above 2 km 0.049 (0.65), land 0.330 (1.0), criteria met 6; the continental crust's net change over the run
  -0.047 against -0.064 (0.006) and the guard's worst depth 10,062 m against 10,840 (under 0.001), since the stamp
  feeds the young orogens' weakness; no step beyond two Earth reliefs, the highest plate elevation 5,610 m (0.69). On
  by default as sourced physics with the guard clean. What stays of the regime far from the fronts is older: stamps 4
  to 30 Myr old lie a median 1,569 km from a flagged front, collisions' orogens outliving their fronts for
  `collision_orogeny_myr`, 30 Myr (PLT-079, a `game-choice`; the code now carries its id). Three seed-chosen weld tests moved seeds (the sweep
  `weld_seed_sweep`, now on the tests' own laws).
- **The collision orogeny's window** (PLT-079, research only, 2026-10-29; a Sonnet research sub-agent, bibliography
  `EnglandThompson1984`, `ThompsonEngland1984`, `Hopkinson2017`, `Weller2021`, `Rey2001`). `collision_orogeny_myr`, 30 Myr,
  sets how long stamped crust stays in the collision regime and locked against being forced under another plate, and
  so which folds, plutons and orogen provinces a run's end places. The sources time these differently. Crustal melt
  (the S-type plutons) begins 20 to 40 Myr after collision (Hopkinson et al. 2017, pp. 58 and 61; the Himalaya's
  leucogranites about 25 to 35 Myr after its 50 ± 10 Ma collision, Weller et al. 2021) and the crust stays hot for tens
  of Myr after (Thompson & England 1984, Fig. 8), so the window ends about where these plutons start. Thrusting goes on
  30 to 50 Myr after a collision's onset (Weller et al. 2021); no source gives a fold window. An orogen erodes over 50
  to 200 Myr (England & Thompson 1984, p. 901). One value cannot serve all three; splitting it by use (the regime and
  lock, the plutons, the provinces) is the lane's next design, and 30 Myr stands until then.
- **Tests.** `the_two_wedges_share_the_crust_by_their_slopes_and_keep_it` (one crest, both slopes, the share within
  0.01 of the formula on 1 km rows, the plateau past the strength height, saturation, ground above a surface),
  `the_two_wedges_raise_the_front_over_a_drowned_edge` (an overriding continent 600 m under the sea: no capped wedge and
  the old belt's toe at the front; with two wedges the crest at the front and the incoming plate's front row raised),
  `stacking_moves_crust_and_creates_none` (two cases added: the crust added is the share of what crossed).

## Plate speed (2026-10-25)

The coordinator's brief for the plate speed lane: CHK-020's `speed_rms_mm_yr` (the plate check's
area-weighted RMS plate speed, averaged over steps) reads about 26 mm/yr on master against its
sourced band of 40 to 100 (Earth about 47 today from Forsyth & Uyeda 1975's Table 1, 50 to 100 over
the last 200 Myr from Zahirovic et al. 2015). It read 41.4 on 2026-10-05, 28.1 on base7 and about 26
on base9 and base10. Find why, from cached runs and unit tests (no new simulations), and fix it
only if the fix is sourced physics or a bug fix: no knob, cap, gain or forcing term (Ben: "Results
that don't align with earth but are still perfectly playable and physics backed > Results that are
forced to align with earth by introducing extremely weird forcing functions").

**The answer.** The level is not a bug and not one merge. It is the force balance's open-loop
calibration of 2026-10-02 (the speed scale 45 mm/yr, PLT-181, which its own row says was "to be
calibrated in task 8 against CHK-020" and never was; the slab and boundary resistances 3 and 3,
PLT-185 and PLT-189, chosen against the open-loop speed targets), with each merge since adding a
resistance or taking a drive away and nothing calibrated again. The largest single fall is the
saturating suction (PLT-540), whose premise no source read supports. Nothing is changed here; the
recommendation at the end is the coordinator's and Ben's to take.

### The level as the design sets it

FRC-016 defines the basal drag coefficient c_b by a reference plate: an oceanic plate of the
average starting plate's area A (a fourteenth of the sphere), pulled by a straight 3,000 km trench
of a full-length 80-Myr slab, its neighbours at rest, moves at the speed scale v_s:
(1 + s + b) c_b A v_s = F_sp L, with s = 3 (slab resistance, PLT-185), b = 3 (boundary resistance,
PLT-189) and v_s = 45 mm/yr. The resistances per metre follow (FRC-017): slab resistance s c_b A / L
per metre of trench against the speed towards it, boundary resistance b c_b A / (2 √(π A)) per metre
of boundary against the relative velocity of the two plates. The slab's terminal velocity is then
v_s (1 + s + b) / s = 105 mm/yr. Every speed in the balance scales with v_s (the drag goes as its
inverse), so the level is linear in it: the diagnosis below gives ×1.49 for ×1.5.

`pairs`). `v_slab` and `v_free` are the check's speeds of the plates with and without a slab.

### The reference plate term by term (the lattice)

`the_reference_plate_on_the_lattice_term_by_term` (plates/tests.rs, 40,000 samples) puts FRC-016's
reference plate on the lattice with `front_pull` on and compares each term's torque in the record
with the continuous cap's (FRC-016's definition on the sphere: basal drag over the cap, slab
resistance along the trench's normal, boundary resistance against the full relative velocity all
round the rim, by quadrature). The lattice moves the plate at 53.2 mm/yr, the continuous cap at
48.7 (the scale is 45; the flat definition on a spherical cap). At the lattice's answer the record
over the cap is: basal drag 0.977 (the plate is 0.976 of A), slab resistance 1.055 and the pull
1.060 (the trench's shares, PLT-560), boundary resistance 0.875 (its metres 0.886 of the rim's
20,615 km: the lattice under-counts the rim). The resisting shares on the lattice are 0.150, 0.487
and 0.362, on the cap 0.149, 0.449 and 0.402 (the flat plate's 1/7, 3/7, 3/7). **The lattice moves
the reference plate faster than the definition, not slower**: no counting of a term on the lattice
slows the planet's plates.

### The planet term by term

`what_sets_the_planets_plate_speed` (plates/tests.rs, ignored; build/speed/diag3.sh on the VM): the
pool's preset `earthlike_quick_16k` at its 100,000 samples, the plate stage alone (no erosion, the
datum's sea) for 600 Myr on two planets, and every 50 Myr after the first 100 the force balance
solved again on the step's state with one term changed, c_b kept unless the row says so. One step's
balance only: the slabs, fronts and collisions a faster motion would make are not in it. The
balance's RMS as CHK-020 weighs it (visible samples, the plates' centroid speeds), then the plates
with a slab pull and the rest; means over the 11 looks. The plate stage alone gives the pool's level
(the motion's RMS 24.9 and 26.4 mm/yr), in about two and a half minutes of test time.

The area with a slab pull is 0.851 and 0.901 of the planet. At 40,000 samples the pattern is the
same (the motion 27.7 and 32.7). `plates_quick_16k` is no guide to the pool's planet: its ridge and
floor (-1,000 and -10,000 m against `earthlike_quick_16k`'s -2,600 and -5,651) give a ridge push
several times Earth's (the motion 39.2 and 40.8 at 100,000 samples, 29.7 and 32.8 with no edge
energy).

What the rows say:

- **The contrast is Earth's, the level is not.** The plates with a slab move about twice as fast as
  the rest (29 to 31 against 15.5), as on Earth (Zahirovic et al. 2015's medians, any subducting
  7.05 cm/yr against 2.6 with no subduction; Forsyth & Uyeda's Table 1, the slab plates 6.1 to 8.6
  cm/yr against 0.7 to 4.2 for the others), but both are short: the pulled plates 0.42 of Zahirovic's
  70.5 mm/yr and the rest 0.60 of 26.
- **The two resistances of the open-loop calibration hold the planet.** At fixed c_b, no boundary
  resistance raises the RMS 1.66 to 1.68 times (the reference plate's 7/4) and no slab resistance
  3.3 to 3.5 times (more than the reference plate's 7/4, since it also takes the suction's link and
  the slabs' terminal velocity with it). The keels, the collision buoyancy and the edge energy each
  move the level by under 10 %.
- **PLT-540 acts mostly as a drag on the plates without a slab.** Not saturating, the suction gives
  the rest 22.4 and 20.0 mm/yr; saturating, 15.5 and 15.5; with no suction at all, 22.0 and 21.1. So
  the link that saturates the suction (to the mantle along the slab's direction, k = share × slab
  resistance × ℓ) slows the overriding plates by more than the whole suction speeds them. That is
  the pool's base4 to base5 step, where only `v_free` fell.
- **Forsyth & Uyeda's force strengths alone raise the level into the band but are not a working
  balance.** Their Table 6 (model X_s, read; PLT-575) put on FRC-016's reference plate gives slab
  resistance 8.94 times the oceanic drag (against the model's 3, with 3 more for the boundary), the
  continental drag 7.9 times the oceanic (the model's keel 3, inside Conrad & Lithgow-Bertelloni
  2006's 2 to 5), the suction 0.078 of the pull and independent of speed (the model's 0.3, saturating),
  a terminal velocity of 72 mm/yr (6.43 / 0.89 cm/yr) and the reference plate at 65 mm/yr against
  the model's 45. Their transform resistance (0.36 per km) and colliding resistance (0.16 per km)
  do not depend on speed and act on transforms and convergent boundaries only; they have no ridge
  resistance and no viscous resistance between plates, so that variant has no boundary resistance.
  It moves the planet at 51 to 60 mm/yr, but the plates without a slab outrun the pulled ones (81 and
  152 against 44 and 47), against Forsyth & Uyeda's own Table 1 and Zahirovic et al.: the
  speed-independent resistances at transforms and collisions, which the viscous all-round boundary
  resistance stood in for, are what holds those plates, and the variant leaves them out.

### What it is and what it is not

- Not a lattice or counting bug: the lattice moves the reference plate faster than its definition.
- Not one merge: the fall from 37 to 27 on the pool is spread over six steps at p < 0.05, five
  down and one up: the largest PLT-540 (-4.9 mm/yr, p < 0.001), then V1 gap 5 (-1.8), V1 gap 2
  (-1.6), PLT-553 (-1.3) and PLT-560 (-0.9), with PLT-561 giving 1.1 back. The fall from 41 on
  2026-10-05 to 37 is the crust budget's.
- The level is the open-loop calibration's, never redone: v_s 45 was not calibrated against CHK-020
  (PLT-181), and s and b were chosen against open-loop targets (CHK-021 to CHK-023, CHK-028) on a
  planet that had none of the fronts, collisions and suction laws since.
- Three places where the model differs from the sources it cites, each read in this lane:
  1. PLT-189 cites Forsyth & Uyeda's transform resistance, but theirs is speed-independent, acts on
     transforms only and has no ridge part; the coded term is viscous and acts on every boundary,
     ridges and trenches included.
  2. The resistance ratios are not Forsyth & Uyeda's (above, and PLT-575).
  3. PLT-540's premise (a slab cannot roll back faster than it sinks, so the mantle resists the
     trench's migration from rest) is `from-memory`, and the trench-migration studies read do not
     support it. In them trench motion follows the upper plate's (V_t about V_up): "spontaneous
     trench rollback related to slab pull is negligible with respect to upper plate motion", and
     92 % of trenches move within ±50 mm/yr (Heuret & Lallemand 2005). The anchor force "is
     inefficient to prevent trench migrations up to ±50 mm.y⁻¹" (Lallemand, Heuret & Boutelier 2005,
     after Heuret & Lallemand). V_t = 0.5 V_sub − 2.3 cm/yr in HS3 (Lallemand et al. 2008), and the
     mean retreat is 1.33 to 1.51 cm/yr (Schellart, Stegman & Freeman 2008). None states a limit of
     rollback by the slab's sinking speed, and the first two say the resistance to migration is
     weak below 50 mm/yr, where PLT-540's resistance has already halved the suction.

### Recommendation (the coordinator's and Ben's; nothing applied)

1. **Physics, recommended: take the force balance's resistances from one source.** As its own lane,
   take Forsyth & Uyeda's Table 6 as a whole: slab resistance 8.94, the continental drag 7.9 (or
   Conrad & Lithgow-Bertelloni's range), the suction speed-independent at 0.078 of the pull (PLT-540
   off). Replace the viscous all-round boundary resistance with their speed-independent transform
   and colliding resistances on those boundaries only, as friction links of the collision link's
   form (k = F / max(|Δv|, floor), `forces.rs`) on the boundary types V1 gap 2 classifies. The
   level then follows from their terminal velocity, and v_s stops being a free number (65 mm/yr on
   the reference plate). The diagnosis shows the first half alone lifts the level into the band and
   lets the free plates run, so the second half is what the lane would build and test: a unit test
   against Forsyth & Uyeda's Table 1 (slab plates 6 to 9 cm/yr, the others 0 to 4) on the lattice,
   then one cumulative arm.
2. **Calibration, Ben's decision: PLT-181's own calibration against CHK-020.** The level is linear in
   v_s: about 68 mm/yr for the band's floor and 80 for Earth's 47. That makes c_b 1.65 to 1.4 ×
   10¹⁴ Pa s/m, an asthenosphere of 1.4 to 1.7 × 10¹⁹ Pa s over 100 km, inside Lithgow-Bertelloni &
   Richards 1998's "of the order of 10^19 Pa s". It is a gain on the level, so under Ben's rule it is
   his to choose, not the lane's.
3. **PLT-540 either way.** Its premise is unsourced and reads against the trench-migration studies,
   it is the largest single fall, and it acts as a drag on the plates without a slab. Option 1 takes
   it off. Off on its own it gives about +2 mm/yr in one step's balance, and its row records the
   speed guard binding on 3 of 24 seeds of the 8k test planet with the fixed share.

## Plate speed, phase 2: Forsyth & Uyeda's balance (PLT-585, 2026-10-25)

The coordinator approved recommendation 1 above and held recommendation 2 (the speed scale's
calibration) for Ben, so `plate_speed_scale_mm_yr` is untouched. The brief: take the drives and
resistances of Forsyth & Uyeda 1975's Table 6 together; build the transform and colliding
resistances as speed-independent friction links of the collision link's form, on transforms and
colliding boundaries only; replace PLT-189's viscous boundary resistance on every boundary, since
its own citation does not support it; turn PLT-540 off in the same change; and let the level follow
from their terminal velocity with no gain or knob added. One switch, unit tests first, on by default
once correct.

The outcome: built, and correct against the paper in its unit tests, but **off by default**. On the
pool (arm `sp-fu`, below) the speed guard (PLT-022) binds in all 8 runs, against none of base12's
24, and CLAUDE.md puts physics on by default only with "no divergence or guard failure on the pool".

### What was built

One switch, `tectonics.forsyth_uyeda_balance` (PLT-585). With it, `forces::Coeffs::new` reads none
of the old law's sizes (`plate_speed_scale_mm_yr`, `slab_resistance`, `boundary_resistance`,
`keel_drag`, `slab_suction_share`, `suction_saturates`): every size is Table 6's (FRC-033) against
the model's reference pull F_sp (3 × 10¹³ N/m at Earth's gravity, FRC-002), which stands for their
6.43 (FRC-034).

| Term | Table 6 (per km; the drags per km² per cm/yr) | In the model |
|---|---|---|
| Slab pull F_SP | 6.43 | F_sp per metre of oceanic front, as before (PLT-182) |
| Slab resistance F_SR | 0.89 per cm/yr | F_sp / v_t per metre of trench, v_t = 6.43 / 0.89 cm/yr = 72.2 mm/yr; on the subducting plate only, against its speed towards the trench (p. 183) |
| Mantle drag F_DF | 0.82 × 10⁻⁵ per cm/yr | the slab resistance per km of trench times 0.82 × 10⁻⁵ / 0.89 per km²: on FRC-016's reference plate the slab resistance is 8.9 times the basal drag (the old law's 3) |
| Continental drag F_CD | 5.65 × 10⁻⁵ per cm/yr | beyond the mantle drag: the keel factor (0.82 + 5.65) / 0.82 = 7.89 (the old law's 3) |
| Suction F_SU | 0.50 | 0.50 / 6.43 = 0.078 of the pull, independent of speed (pp. 170-171, 195; the old law's 0.3; PLT-540 not read) |
| Transform resistance F_TF | 0.36, against the relative motion | a friction link of 0.36 / 6.43 F_sp per metre on transforms |
| Colliding resistance F_CR | 0.16, against the relative motion | a friction link of 0.16 / 6.43 F_sp per metre on colliding boundaries, trenches and collision fronts alike ("no distinction between the resisting force at trenches and the resisting force at mountain belts", p. 170) |
| Ridge push F_RP | 0.36 | not taken: the model's column energy stays (PLT-187), about 0.10 of the pull at the pool preset's ridge and old floor against Table 6's 0.056 |
| (viscous boundary resistance) | not in their model | none (PLT-189 is not read) |

The collision resistance (the belt's weight and the dragged-down crust's buoyancy, FRC-018, FRC-030)
and the edge energy are kept: they are the model's physics for what Table 6 lumps into F_CR and F_RP,
and the brief named only the transform and colliding resistances. The speed guard (PLT-022,
250 mm/yr) is unchanged.

**The friction links** (FRC-035). Forsyth & Uyeda's F_TF and F_CR are forces per unit length "opp.
rel. motion" whatever the speed, acting "with equal strength on both plates" (p. 169). Each is a
link between the two plates at the boundary sample along their relative velocity, of coefficient
k = F / max(|Δv|, floor) with FRC-011's floor of 1 mm/yr, `Balance::add_friction`, the collision
link's form: linearised about the step's motion, so the fixed point the motion relaxes to is the
plastic answer, and a drive smaller than the friction leaves the boundary slipping under the floor.

**Which boundary is which.** Forsyth & Uyeda's own rule, the one their strengths were fitted with
(p. 183): "We have arbitrarily chosen φ = 60° ... as the dividing point between classifying a
boundary segment as a convergent boundary, I_CR, or as a transform fault, I_TF", φ = tan⁻¹(V_PAR /
V_PER) (`forces::fu_transform`). So a segment within 30 degrees of strike-slip is a transform; one
whose plates converge across it otherwise is colliding; one where they part has no friction (they
have no ridge resistance). V1 gap 2's boundary types (Bird's 20 degrees, PLT-311) are not used here.

**Where it acts.** A trench's friction is counted once, at the front the overriding sample has, over
the front's metres (PLT-560's share of the straight front), as its pull and suction are, against the
plate going under. Every other stretch of boundary with a visible plate beyond it counts from both
sides, half of its share each (PLT-530), by its own normal (PLT-310); the side going under in an
active contact skips it, since its front counts it. The first build counted every boundary by the
visible-neighbour rule alone and missed most trenches: at a mature trench the subducting plate's
samples beside the trench have gone under and see no other plate, and the overriding plate's front
sample was skipped as a front, so a small plate over a trench had no friction at all. The force
record books the friction in its `boundary_resistance` column.

**PLT-540 and the pinned fixtures.** PLT-540 (`suction_saturates`) is not read under PLT-585
(`Coeffs::new`), so one switch chooses the whole law: Forsyth & Uyeda's suction is independent of
speed, and PLT-540's premise is `from-memory` and unsupported by the trench-migration studies read
(above). The brief turned PLT-540 off in the same change; with PLT-585 off by default, turning it
off by itself would change the default planet with nothing in its place, so it stays on with the
old law. The lattice reference tests (`the_reference_plate_on_the_lattice_*`, `old_law()`) test the
speed scale's own law, and the 8k test planet's collision, suture and recording fixtures pin the old
law (`forsyth_uyeda_balance` false, `suction_saturates` true) whatever the defaults are: under
PLT-585 the guard binds on that planet (below).

### Unit tests against the paper (`forces.rs`)

- `the_resistances_are_forsyth_and_uyedas_table_6`: the slab's terminal velocity 72.2 mm/yr against
  the paper's "7.0 cm/yr" (p. 189; their "(= 5.65/0.82)" is the ratio of their two drags, 6.43 /
  0.89 is 7.2), within 5 %; the continental drag 7.89 times the oceanic ("approximately eight
  times", p. 189); the suction and the two frictions their shares of the pull; the slab resistance
  8.9 times the drag on FRC-016's reference plate; none of the old law's settings read, PLT-540
  included.
- `the_reference_plate_moves_near_its_slabs_terminal_velocity`: FRC-016's reference plate (the
  starting plates' mean area, 3,000 km of trench of a full-length 80-Myr slab) moves at 66.3 mm/yr
  without friction (65.1 by v_t s / (1 + s), s = 9.15, on a flat plate) and at 56.1 mm/yr with
  friction all round its rim, after 13 solves; Forsyth & Uyeda's plates attached to a slab move at
  "6-9 cm/year" (p. 178), their terminal velocity "roughly coincident with the average velocity of
  oceanic plates attached to a slab" (p. 189). On the cap the 60 degree rule makes 84 of the rim's
  187 samples transforms and 103 colliding; the friction as fixed forces against the motion gives
  the same answer.
- `friction_resists_with_its_force_whatever_the_speed`: a drive larger than the friction moves the
  plate as a fixed force would; a smaller one leaves it under the floor speed.
- `friction_holds_back_a_plate_with_no_slab`: the runaway the diagnosis found. A plate of the
  reference plate's size with no slab, pushed by a ridge along the back 140 degrees of its rim at the
  pool preset's ridge and floor: the old law 19.2 mm/yr; Table 6 without friction 146.2 (the
  runaway); with friction 37.6; at Table 6's own ridge push (0.36 per km) 0.81, held at the floor
  ("continental drag is the primary regulator of the velocity of plates not attached to downgoing
  slabs", p. 190). Continental: the old law 12.5, with friction 4.8.

The terminal-velocity test builds its own trench on a cap and reads no lattice fronts, so it does
not depend on the front set (the front lane's current-geometry fronts change only the planet's).

### The planet (one step's balance, iterated to its fixed point)

`what_sets_the_planets_plate_speed` again (build/speed/diag7.sh), the same two planets and looks as
above (`earthlike_quick_16k`, 100,000 samples, the plate stage alone, 11 looks from 100 to 600 Myr),
the friction iterated to its fixed point at each look:

| Variant | Supercontinent, seed 1: RMS / pulled / rest | Scattered continents, seed 2 |
|---|---|---|
| the old law (PLT-585 off, PLT-540 on) | 26.7 / 27.7 / 19.5 | 28.5 / 29.6 / 15.5 |
| Table 6 without the friction (phase 1's row) | 62.7 / 42.3 / 134.6 | 54.1 / 45.6 / 94.7 |
| **Forsyth & Uyeda's balance (PLT-585)** | **50.2 / 36.4 / 97.0** | **44.2 / 38.3 / 68.7** |
| PLT-585 at Table 6's ridge push (the edge energy scaled to 0.056 of the pull) | 41.2 / 32.4 / 69.6 | 33.1 / 34.2 / 21.9 |

The level is in CHK-020's band with no knob, and the pulled plates move at 36 to 38 mm/yr (the old
law's 28 to 30). The friction takes the plates without a slab from 135 and 95 to 97 and 69 mm/yr,
but not down to the pulled plates' speed: the contrast Forsyth & Uyeda's Table 1 and Zahirovic et al.
2015 show (slab plates two to three times the others) is reversed on the planet.

**Why: the overriding oceanic plates.** The rest's RMS² is mostly oceanic plates of 0.1 to 0.5
starting plates (0.65 and 0.51 of it). They lie over trenches. Table 6's suction draws an overriding
plate with 0.50 per km of trench, its colliding resistance at the same trench holds it with 0.16, the
slab resistance acts only on the plate going under ("the component of motion of the plate relative
to the mantle which is directed perpendicular to the strike of the trench", p. 183, for the
subducting plate), and nothing else in their model resists the overriding plate's advance but the
friction on its other boundaries. So 0.34 per km of trench, plus its ridge push, less that friction,
against the basal drag alone, 0.82 × 10⁻⁵ per km² per cm/yr: its speed goes as its trench length
over its area, as 1 / R. Forsyth & Uyeda's Earth had one such plate, the Caribbean (Table 1: 3.8 ×
10⁶ km², no continent, 2.4 cm/yr, 3,700 km of trench it overrides, 4,400 km of transform and 4,400 km
of convergent boundary), and on Table 6 its friction holds it: 0.36 × 4,400 + 0.16 × 4,400 = 2,288
against a suction of 0.50 × 3,700 = 1,850, 1.24 times (computed). Their other plates without a slab
are continental (Eurasia, North America, Africa, Antarctica), held by the continental drag. Their
own words on the term: "In view of the uncertainty of the nature of F_SU, in the present paper we
modelled it to be velocity independent and perpendicular to the trench, although F_SU caused by the
secondary flow may be proportional to the descent rate of the slab" (pp. 170-171); models with the
suction proportional to the slab's descent or to the convergence gave "similar" results (p. 195);
"The least understood part of our model is the nature of this suction force" (p. 193). Nothing here
changes it: the brief was Table 6 as a whole.

### The speed guard

On the 8k test planet (`plates_quick_16k`, whose ridge push is several times Earth's;
`weld_seed_sweep`, 300 Myr, seeds 1 to 24) the guard binds on all 24 scattered seeds and 22 of 24
supercontinent seeds, 3 to 146 plate-steps a run (under the old law: 0 of the 24 scattered seeds at
PLT-540's arm). On `earthlike_quick_16k` at 8,000 samples (`where_the_speed_guard_binds`, 300 Myr)
it binds 0, 21 and 5 plate-steps on scattered 2, supercontinent 4 and scattered 1. The plates it
holds are the overriding oceanic plates above: no slab pull, the suction about equal to the basal
drag, and on the smallest (a few samples) a balance answer above 1,000 mm/yr. The collision, suture
and recording tests on the 8k test planet keep the old law: only supercontinent 11 of the 48 runs
both welds and stays clear of the guard, and the recording test asserts the guard never binds.

**PLT-582 had not reached the force balance** (noted 2026-10-26). sp-fu2 and sp-fu3 were read as if
the current-geometry fronts held throughout, but PLT-582's test was applied by the arcs' fronts and
the boundary mix only. The force balance gathered its fronts from the frozen lattice until
2026-10-26 ("The force balance's front on the current geometry (2026-10-26)" below), so these arms'
slab pull, suction and friction stood on the stale fronts. The plates that bound under PLT-585 were
small overriding plates drawn by suction, which attaches at the same fronts; how much of their
binding was the stale fronts' was not measured.

**The boundaries by the 60 degree rule** (a VM-only probe at PLT-585's fixed point on the same two
planets as above, not committed). Of the planet's boundary, 0.28 to 0.29 is transform, 0.56 to 0.58
converging and 0.13 to 0.15 diverging; Earth's by Table 1 is 30 % transform, 34 % convergent and 35 %
ridge (ridge 1,183, transform 1,016, convergent 1,136, × 100 km; computed). So the planet has
Earth's share of transforms; it has less ridge and more converging boundary. The free oceanic plates
(0.1 to 0.5 starting plates) hold, all together, 1.11 to 1.23 times their suction in friction, near
the Caribbean's 1.24; the fast ones hold 0.43 to 0.67 times: long trench and few transforms. Their
speed is about (0.50 − 0.16) × trench over the basal drag times their area. The probe may count too
much trench where the overriding plate meets crust it cannot see (a hidden neighbour), so the fast
plates' ratio is a lower bound.

**What would hold them, with no knob.** On Earth an overriding plate whose trench retreats opens a
marginal sea behind its arc, and then "the oceanward migration of trench-arc system becomes an
inefficient means of generating suction on the continental plate behind the marginal sea" (p. 170):
the arc's sliver moves with the trench and the plate behind it does not. The model's plates are
rigid and do not split along an arc, so the whole small plate follows the suction. Two physical
routes, neither built: back-arc opening (an overriding plate splits at its arc when its suction
outruns its own drag, so the sliver that moves is small and bounded by the new ridge's spreading),
or a suction law with a source (pp. 170-171: "may be proportional to the descent rate of the slab";
PLT-540's saturating law is a version of this, but its premise is `from-memory`). Until one of them
is built, PLT-585 stays a switch that is off.

**With incipient subduction (the front lane's switch).** The front lane is building incipient
subduction (Gurnis et al. 2004; decisions log 2026-10-25) behind its own switch: a contact stays
incipient until its slab reaches 100 km, and until then its front resists with a plastic 2.5 × 10¹²
N/m (5 × 10¹¹ at a ridge), linearised as the collision term is, and builds no arc. That is a
friction-like resistance on a converging front, and PLT-585's colliding resistance F_CR acts on the
same front (a trench's friction is counted at the overriding sample's front, above). With both
switches on, the rule is: **an incipient contact's front takes the incipient resistance alone, and
PLT-585's friction (F_CR, or F_TF where the 60 degree rule calls the front a transform) only once the
contact is mature.** Forsyth & Uyeda fitted F_CR on Earth's mature trenches and mountain belts
("no distinction between the resisting force at trenches and the resisting force at mountain belts",
p. 170), and the incipient resistance is the whole resistance of a front whose slab has not yet
formed, so counting both on one front counts that front's resistance twice. In size, F_CR is 0.16 /
6.43 × 3 × 10¹³ = 7.5 × 10¹¹ N/m (computed), so the incipient front resists 3.4 times as hard as a
mature one, and 0.67 times at a ridge. The code is two conditions in the friction pass of
`forces.rs` (`if friction`): the front's link is skipped while its contact is incipient, and the
loop over the other boundaries skips a plate that holds an incipient contact with the sample's plate
from either side, so neither side adds a half share in its place. The front lane landed second and
added them (2026-10-25), with the unit test `an_incipient_front_takes_no_forsyth_uyeda_friction`
(both switches on: an incipient front carries the incipient resistance alone, the same as with
PLT-585 off, and no friction between its two plates; a mature one F_CR alone, from the overriding
side, and no incipient resistance; the other boundaries' friction the same in both). The incipient
contacts are the ones the arcs and the boundary mix read, by the slab before the step's growth. A
continental sample at an incipient contact's front takes no incipient resistance (it is a
collision's, PLT-610), so it keeps the front's friction there as at a mature contact.
