that: the suturing zones 1.75 to 2.45, of it PLT-242's share 0.30 to 0.50, "no room" left over 0.41
to 0.68 and "no room" at the strength height 1.04 to 1.27. The collision front at any time grew from
9,419 to 12,153 km, its convergence from 21.0 to 26.5 mm/yr and the area crossing it from 0.198 to
0.322 km²/yr. Sediment subduction takes 0.30 (1.18 to 1.48), subduction erosion 0.16 (0.35 to 0.51;
erosive fronts 7,530 to 12,062 km), and resampling 0.06. Net −1.12 to −1.79 km³/yr, the budget's
other parts making up the rest. Coast with high ground rose with the belts (the felsic rock they
make 3.75 to 6.66 km³/yr, the continental volume they add 4.30 to 7.68), with the higher continental
arcs (their median 814 to 1,062 m) and with less continental crust under a lower sea.

**Parked.** The guard is not clean, so by Ben's condition the default stays 45 (the coordinator's
ruling of 2026-10-26). CLAUDE.md's default-on rule asks for no guard failure on the pool, PLT-022 is
a guard that should never bind, and PLT-585 was kept off for the same reason. Branch
`speed-scale-75-parked` holds the 75 in params.rs and the 13 presets, with the two tests that now
read the scale instead of pinning 45. (PLT-582's amendment cleared the guard on the pool later the
same day, but on the test planet 75 still binds it on many seeds where 45 binds on none, so 75
stays parked: "The force balance's front on the current geometry" below. 75 went on later that day
with the ridge push by the floor's age: "The ridge push by the floor's age (PLT-684, 2026-10-26)".)

**What binds** (measured from the arm's records; no fix built). Three of the four plates that bound
were born by subduction initiation and were being consumed down their own trench: scattered 1 plates
68 and 81, supercontinent 1 plate 201. Their slab pull stayed at full size while the visible front
fell 5 to 7 times and the area 10 to 300 times. Plate 68 pulled 2,175 × 10²⁴ N m on a 10,854 km
front at 2,691 samples, and 1,496 on 1,642 km at 95 samples. At the binds their pull per metre of
current front was 5.5 to 14.3 × 10¹³ N/m. That is beyond the law's most, FRC-002's 3 × 10¹³ times
FRC-004's 1.5. At two binds plate 201 had no current front at all (2 samples).

The cause is in the code. The force balance (forces.rs) reads a front from any lattice neighbour of
a plate with an active contact, hidden or carried away. PLT-582's test (a visible sample of the
subducting plate within two spacings now) is applied by the arcs' fronts (subduction.rs) and by the
boundary mix, but not by the force balance. Between resamplings the lattice is frozen, so a consumed
plate keeps pulling along its trench as it stood at the last resampling, while its basal drag goes
with its area. Its slab resistance sits on the same stale front, so the remnant moves at the old
trench's terminal velocity (pull × speed / slab resistance 180 to 213 mm/yr for plate 68). It also
turns: plate 68 from about 8 to about 39 degrees per Myr as it went from 408 to 95 samples, and
plate 201 at 2 samples some 2,000 to 3,000 before the guard (an RMS of 2,034 mm/yr on a plate of
about 57 km radius) and 250 under it.

The fourth plate (supercontinent 4 plate 197, 1,258 to 1,636 samples) pulls inside the law (3.2 ×
10¹³ N/m). It is a slab plate at the old law's terminal velocity, the scale × (1 + 3 + 3) / 3 × the
slab's weight (175 × about 1.3 at 75). Its centroid moves at 166 to 190 mm/yr and its basal drag is
3 to 6 % of its resistance. Forsyth & Uyeda's slab plates move at about one speed whatever their
area (Table 1: Cocos 8.6 cm/yr at 2.9 × 10⁶ km², Nazca 7.6 at 15, Pacific 8.0 at 108; p. 177: "The
Nazca, Cocos and Pacific plates are moving about the same velocity"). The old law's basal drag, a
seventh of the reference plate's resistance, instead spreads the slab plates from the scale (the
reference plate) up to 7/3 of it times the weight (a plate with a long trench for its area).

Over all plate-steps, the pull beyond the law's most on the current front is small: 1.7 % of all
pull on base17-s4 and 2.7 % on the arm. The sp-fu arms above (PLT-585) were read with this force
balance; PLT-582 did not reach it.

## The force balance's front on the current geometry (2026-10-26)

PLT-582 (2026-10-25, "The front on the current geometry" above) made a front stand only while a
visible sample of the subducting plate is within `subduction::trench_row_rad` (two spacings) of
the overriding sample now. The arcs' fronts (`subduction::fronts_begin`) and the boundary mix asked
it; the force balance (`forces.rs`, `balance_step`) did not. It gathered a front from any lattice
neighbour of a plate with an active contact, hidden or carried on. Between resamplings the lattice
is frozen, so a plate being consumed down its trench kept its pull, its suction and its slab
resistance on the trench as it stood at the last resampling, while its basal drag shrank with its
area. That was what bound PLT-022's guard on three of the four plates in the arm sp-v75 ("Speed
scale 75, the calibration's first read" above).

The amendment (PLT-582, the coordinator's call of 2026-10-26) asks the force balance the same test,
by the same code (`subduction::SlabBeside`, over a k-d tree of the step's positions):

- **A front** counts a subducting neighbour only while a visible sample of its plate stands within
  the row. The slab pull, the suction, the slab resistance, the incipient resistance (PLT-610) and a
  collision's resistance act at the fronts, with Forsyth & Uyeda's front friction (PLT-585), so all
  of them follow. So does the slab's growth, which the fronts' convergence feeds.
- **A hanging slab** (no front this step) pulls only at samples with a visible sample of the
  subducting plate within the row.
- **A collision's incoming side** (a continental sample on the subducting side, which takes no
  edge energy) counts the overriding plate only within the row.

The rest of the edge pass is unchanged: its outward direction, the boundary resistance's links and
the friction away from a front still read every lattice neighbour. They resist and do not drive. It
rides on `tectonics.front_current_geometry` (on): off, the force balance reads the lattice as
before, as the fronts and the mix do.

**The test** (`a_consumed_plates_pull_falls_with_its_visible_trench`, written first): the ocean
plate of `a_consumed_slab_leaves_no_front`, 3 spacings deep and 30 degrees long, given a slab at full
depth and driven under the continent at 50 mm/yr until none of it is visible (20,000 samples, 9
steps). Before the amendment the pull stayed at full size with no trench left (5.46 × 10²⁶ N m at the
first step, 6.14 × 10²⁶ at the last with no front, the slab's weight growing with its age), and the
test failed on its "on" assertion. After it, with the rule off and on:

| Step | Fronts on the current geometry | Pull off, 10²⁶ N m | Pull on | Suction off | Suction on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 24 | 5.457 | 5.457 | 1.637 | 1.637 |
| 3 | 24 | 5.635 | 5.635 | 1.691 | 1.691 |
| 4 | 22 | 5.723 | 5.319 | 1.717 | 1.596 |
| 5 | 15 | 5.809 | 3.672 | 1.743 | 1.101 |
| 6 to 9 | 0 | 5.894 to 6.141 | 0 | 1.768 to 1.842 | 0 |

On the live margin the pull is the same off and on; on the way down it falls with the visible
trench (step 5: 0.67 of the first step's for 0.63 of its fronts); with no trench it is gone.

the transfer's own return, and `motion_set_by` reads it. The unit test

did nothing sets no motion). PLT-080's note.

## The ridge push by the floor's age (PLT-684, 2026-10-26)

**What it answers.** At a speed scale of 75 the test planet's sweep bound PLT-022's guard on small
plates whose balance asked 111 to 600 mm/yr of them (above, "The test planet's guard"). The
coordinator's brief for the stage (2026-10-26): find the physics the balance gets wrong on small
plates and fix it from sources, so that 75 can go on with the guard clean; no cap, no speed limit,
no forcing term and no size-dependent factor, since the bind is the symptom.

**The decomposition.** The sweep's 56 binds (PLT-582, the scale at 75, A and B, the motion fix;
`plates_quick_16k` at 8,000 samples, 300 Myr, seeds 1 to 24, each start) were taken apart with a
test-only trace of `balance_step`: per plate-step the visible samples, the boundary by class
(trench, overriding, collision, incipient, transform, opening), each term's force (slab pull,
suction, the edge term's net force), each resistance's coefficient (basal drag, slab resistance,
boundary resistance, collision, suction) and the speed each term alone would give against the
plate's total resistance. The same trace ran at 45 for every plate-step, the comparison of a free
plate of the same size.

- The edge term carried the bound plates: its median share of the balance's answer along its
  direction was 0.79, the slab pull's 0.16, and 44 of the 56 had the edge term as their largest
  driver (12 the pull). The bound plates were small (median 45 visible samples) with long boundaries
  for their area.
- The model already resists a small plate by its boundary, as Forsyth & Uyeda's balance does
  (PLT-585): under 50 visible samples the boundary resistance (PLT-189, per metre of boundary) is
  17.7 times the basal drag (per area) and the slab resistance (PLT-185, per metre of trench) 54
  times; over 1,000 samples 1.1 and 0.5 times. No resistance that scales with boundary length was
  missing.
- Later work on small plates agrees that their edges, not their base, hold them (a Sonnet lookup,
  abstracts only: the full texts were behind publishers' walls). Conrad & Hager 1999: "Earth's
  plate velocities are not correlated to plate size". Neves, Searle & Bott 2003, on oceanic
  microplates: "At most, the basal drag comprises 20% of the force resisting microplate rotation".
  Schouten, Klitgord & Gallo 1993: a microplate's rotation "could be driven by the drag of the Nazca
  and Pacific plates on the microplate's edges". Forsyth & Uyeda 1975: slab-attached plates move at
  a terminal velocity "regardless of the other features of the trailing horizontal part of the
  plates". Becker & O'Connell 2001: parameterized edge forces "does not significantly improve the
  model fit". The abstracts of Conrad & Lithgow-Bertelloni 2002 and 2004 say nothing of size.
- What the source scales otherwise is a driving term counted per metre of boundary: the edge term's
  column energy. `plates_quick_16k` (the test planet's preset) has its crest at −1,000 m and sinks
  its floor by Cortial's dampening towards −10,000 m (PLT-129), and the edge term read the depth
  below the crest down to that old floor (FRC-021). Old floor counted 9 km below its crest, a ridge
  push of 2.7 × 10¹³ N/m, 8.7 times what 3,051 m of thermal subsidence gives (3.05 × 10¹² N/m) and
  about ten times Copley et al.'s figure. Every plate with a ridge on one side and old floor
  elsewhere took that edge force per metre of its boundary, while its drag went with its area.

Variants on the same sweep (the trace's switches, test-only; guarded plate-steps at 75, all 0 at 45):

| Variant | binds at 75 |
|---|---|
| the test planet as it was (PLT-582 + 75 + A and B) | 56 (20 scattered, 36 supercontinent) |
| the depth below the crest clamped at 3,051 m | 1 |
| GDH1's crest and floor in the preset (−2,600 and −5,651 m) | 2 |
| `earthlike_quick_16k`'s tectonics on the test planet | 3, on 2 seeds |

**What the sources say.** Turcotte & Schubert's ridge push, which FRC-012 writes as −C d², is the
cooled lithosphere's: d is the column's thermal subsidence, which the plate model stops at about
80 Myr. Read for this stage (a Sonnet sub-agent, full texts unless noted):

- Copley, Avouac & Royer 2010 (JGR 115, B03410): the ridge push "estimated using a plate cooling
  model", "integrating ... the potential energy differences due to cooling (using the seafloor age
  distribution)"; "line force is taken to be 3 x 10^12 N per unit length", "2.5 - 3 x 10^12 N/m".
- ETH Zurich lecture notes, chapter 6.2: "ridge push force is linearly proportional to the age t",
  "80 Ma ... 3.1 x 10^12 N/m".
- Doin & Fleitout 1996 (EPSL 142:121): "In the plate model the subsidence is stopped at an age of
  about 80 Ma".
- Clennett et al. 2023 (Sci. Rep. 13:10191): ΔU from the age-depth law and isostasy, not from
  measured bathymetry; the plate model leaves half-space cooling after 81 Ma.
- Sandiford, "trench pull" (EarthArXiv preprint): "2-4 TN m^-1 ... applicable to the subsidence of
  old lithosphere"; the trench's flexure is a force of its own, measured against "an isostatic
  reference column of the same age".
- Sandwell's lecture notes: the ridge push is the force of isostatically compensated topography.
- Against the age form: Zoback & Zoback (Treatise on Geophysics 6.06), 1 to 5 × 10¹² N/m
  "calculated directly from bathymetry". On Earth's floor away from trenches the two agree, since
  bathymetry follows the age-depth law; on the plate-only presets the floor follows Cortial's
  game-choice relaxation instead, and at a trench the depth is the slab's and flexure's.
- Forsyth & Uyeda 1975 (read before): McKenzie 1972's ridge push "of the order of 300 bars", 2.4 ×
  10¹² N/m over 80 km.
- Not reachable: Parsons & Richter 1980, Lister 1975, Turcotte & Schubert.

**The law (`tectonics.ridge_push_by_age`, on by default).** The sea floor's column energy reads its
depth below the crest at most as deep as GDH1 sinks floor of its age, d ≤ d_GDH1(t) − 2,600 m
(PLT-352, FRC-036): 0 at the ridge, 1,154 m at 10 Myr, 1,632 m at 20, 2,898 m at 100, towards
3,051 m. Ground deeper than that (a trench in young floor, a flexural moat, the plate-only presets'
deep floor) has its age's energy; ground shallower (sediment, a seamount, a plateau) keeps its own
depth, so a load on old floor still pushes less. The age is the sample's crust age at the step.
Land keeps its Airy column (FRC-014). The bound acts in the plate's mean energy, at each boundary
sample and in a belt's weight. On the Earth-like presets the old bound (the preset's floor, 3,051 m
below the crest) and the new one meet on old floor, so there the law changes only young floor that
stands deeper than its age. Off, the depth is read down to the preset's old floor, as before.

The unit test `the_sea_floor_s_ridge_push_is_its_age_s_thermal_subsidence`: the subsidence 0 at the
ridge, 365 √10 m at 10 Myr, within 0.5 m of 365 √20 at 20, 2,897 to 2,899 m at 100 and 3,051 m at
1,000; old floor's push C × 3,051² = 3.05 × 10¹² N/m, inside 2.4 to 3.5 × 10¹²; the plate-only
presets' −10 km floor at 400 Myr has old floor's energy (to 1e-4) and, unbounded, 8.70 ± 0.01 times
it; a 10-Myr trench at −8,000 m has −C × 365² × 10; a loaded floor at −4,000 m keeps −C × 1,400²;
land is unchanged; through the switch, off gives −C × 9,000² for the deep floor.
`friction_holds_back_a_plate_with_no_slab` reads the model's push from the same energy.

## The overriding plate's share (PLT-652, 2026-10-25)

The collision-front diagnosis (build log 2026-10-25, "Front lane: what sets the crust added per km of
collision front") found base14's fronts carrying Earth's crust per km (1.16 times Bird's CCB over the
run) but keeping 0.89 of it within 400 km of the front, where the planet stacks 1.81 times Earth's
excess crust per km and 2.8 times its crust over 55 km. Earth's overriding plates take much of a
collision's convergence away from the front: of Arabia's 440 km since 22 Ma, 135 km went into the
Zagros and 230 km into Central Iran and the Alborz behind it (52 %, Mouthereau 2011), and Asia took
600 to 1,050 km of India's convergence beside the Himalaya's 450 to 900 (an Asia share of 0.40 to 0.70,
van Hinsbergen et al. 2011, Tectonics). The model's overriding plate had no way to do that.

### The law (`tectonics.collision_upper_plate_shortening`)

The continental lithosphere deforms as a thin viscous sheet (England & McKenzie 1982; Houseman &
England 1986), so where it shortens is set by its strength, and the model already has that strength:
PLT-414's sheet, ε̇ = ΔU / (4 η L), with PLT-415's η = η_0 e^(t_eq / τ_s) at the lithosphere's thermal
age (ISO-112). PLT-652 puts the belt's push where ΔU stands:

- **The push.** A mountain range pushes on the lowland beside it with its gravitational potential
  energy over the lowland's (Molnar & Lyon-Caen 1988: Tibet's 6 to 7 × 10¹² N/m). That is the
  balance's edge term (FRC-018) read across the belt (`forces::belt_push_n_m`): the mean column
  energy of the belt's continental samples (within the belt's 400 km of the front) over the mean of
  the interior's strip (below), the lowland it pushes on. A 5 km belt pushes with 6.7 × 10¹² N/m, a belt at the 40 MPa strength height (1.46 km)
  with about 1.5 × 10¹².
- **The interior** behind the belt carries that push as a thin sheet. Along the strip behind the
  front (the overriding plate's visible continental samples beyond the belt's 400 km, between the
  front's ends along it and not ahead of it), each column shortens at ε̇ = F / (4 η L), so the
  interior shortens at v = F / (4 η_0 L) ∫ w dx, with w = η_0 / η = e^(−t_eq / τ_s) (PLT-470's
  form). At w = 1 that is 158 mm/yr per 1,000 km of strip for 2 × 10¹³ N/m, 53 mm/yr for a 5 km
  belt's push.
- **The share.** The interior takes v / v_n of the convergence, at most all of it. That share of the
  crust the step keeps goes to the strip's columns in proportion to T w (each column thickens by its
  own strain), the rest to the wedge and the belt by their own rules (PLT-242's share, PLT-600 and
  PLT-601's taper, PLT-253's strength height unchanged).

There is no share constant and no new value: η_0 (10²² Pa s), τ_s (62.8 Myr) and L (100 km) are
PLT-414's and PLT-415's, the column energy and the edge scale the balance's. The belt sets its own
height. A fresh front has no belt and no push, so the front takes the first step; the belt then
rises until its push drives the interior at the rest of the convergence, which is how a thin sheet
grows a plateau in front of an indenter (England & Houseman 1986). The weakness sets where that
balance falls. A start continent's keel (200 km, `thermal_keel_km`) has t_eq 384 Myr and w 0.0022;
a lithosphere of 150 km has w 0.078, of 120 km 0.23, and the hot limit (60 km) 1. So a keeled
craton behind a front takes almost nothing even under a belt at its strength height, and a hot,
thinned plate takes most or all under a low belt. Crust is conserved: the interior's crust is the
crossing's mix, counted in `kept` and in its own column of the crust budget (`upper`).

In the unit fixture (a head-on collision at 30 mm/yr, the overriding continent's strip about 2,050 km
deep behind the belt), the twelfth step's share is 0.008 at 200 km of lithosphere under a push of
6.6 × 10¹² N/m, 0.055 at 180, 0.14 at 165, 0.25 at 150, 0.55 at 120 and 0.82 at 60 under 1.4 × 10¹²
N/m: behind the hot plate the belt stays low. Over the twelve steps the 60 km interior took 0.67 of the
crust kept, the 200 km one 0.006.

The push is not the collision's resistance in the balance. The balance resists a collision with the
edge term and the buoyancy of the continental lithosphere dragged down (FRC-030), a plastic
resistance whose capacity grows with the shortening to about 9 × 10¹³ N/m at the slab's full depth.
That buoyancy is the mantle's hold on the slab, not a horizontal force carried by the overriding
plate, and it is an order of magnitude over what a range pushes with. The first build read it as
the force on the interior: in the unit fixture the force grew by 6.5 × 10¹² N/m a step with the
shortening, and a plate of 150 km took all of the convergence from the fourth step. That reading
was dropped before any arm ran.

Two choices are this lane's, neither a fitted value. The strip is one-dimensional: it carries the
front's force undiminished to the plate's far side, where a two-dimensional sheet spreads a
boundary's stress over a length scale of the order of the boundary's width (England, Houseman &
Sonder 1985, from memory), so the share is the interior's largest. And the law is kinematic: the
balance's resistance and the plates' motion are as before; only where the crust goes changes. The interior's columns
are stamped as a collision orogeny (fold along the front), so the collapse, the root removal and
the erosion treat them as such, but they stay out of the belt's record (its height, width and
footprint are the front's).

### The interior as a 2-D sheet (PLT-733, 2026-10-29)

**Why.** On base30 (master d850490b, 24 runs, the crust-budget maps 50 Myr before each run's end)
the coast with high ground by v1census version 1's rule is 0.178; 0.342 of all the coast lies within
150 km of a collision belt, those coasts hold 0.695 of the high coasts, and without them coast_hi
would be 0.049. The collision high coasts face their own plate's sea (0.789 of them; ocean floor a
median 51 Myr old), lie on an overriding plate (0.890), a median 590 km behind the collision front,
with their high ground (Himalayan, 0.870) a median 569 km behind it. The fronts are short against
the continents behind them: a median 306 km along strike (771 km length-weighted, 1,133 km at the
90th percentile). So the high coasts are the far coasts of overriding plates whose interiors the
collision thickened: the 1-D strip above carries the belt's push undiminished to the plate's far
side.

**The law.** A thin viscous sheet driven over a boundary segment responds over a length set by the
segment, not the sheet. England, Houseman & Sonder 1985 (the abstract; their equations were not
seen): with the velocity normal to the boundary "the deformation field decays away from the
boundary with a characteristic length scale 1/3 to 1/10 the wavelength of the imposed boundary
velocity distribution for n between 1 and 10", the lengths decreasing "approximately as n^-1/2".
Ježek et al. 2002 (eq. 1, p. 95, after England et al. 1985, Ar = 0) write it as
v(y) = v0 exp(−(π√n / 2L) y) with L the indenter's width, and England et al. 2016 (Sect. 3.2,
Appendix A1.2) give a strain rate reach of about w/√n for a stress or velocity condition over a
length w, and for a Newtonian sheet driven as cos(πy/2w) an e-fold of 4w/π. With the switch
`tectonics.collision_upper_decay` the strip is read that way: a column x behind the front (along
the front's mean normal, from its foremost edge sample) takes the share in proportion to
T w e^(−x/L), the interior's rate is F / (4 η_0 L_lith) ∫ w e^(−x/L) dx, and the lowland the belt
pushes on is the strip's column energy weighted by e^(−x/L). L = 2W/π, W the front's extent along
strike: a third of the wavelength 2W, the abstract's figure for n = 1, which is the sheet law's own
(PLT-414's ε̇ = F / (4 η L) is linear). Earth's lithosphere fits India-Asia with n of 3 or more
(England & Houseman 1986, abstract), which would shorten L by √3; the model's law is the linear one,
so its own n stands. The 1985 solutions are for Ar = 0: the gravitational spreading that lengthens
the deformation with Ar (Houseman & England 1986) is the surface stage's and the collapse's
(PLT-414) here, which spread a thickened column after the plate stage has placed it.

The project's readings: the front's extent along strike is the indenter's width; the strain rate,
the velocity's gradient, decays as the velocity does; x is measured along the front's mean normal.
In the unit fixture (a cap 60 degrees across, its front about 6,700 km long, so L is about 4,200 km)
the interior takes less crust with the switch and lays its rise nearer the front
(`the_two_dimensional_sheet_keeps_the_interiors_crust_near_the_front`).

**On the pool (arm up-decay, 2026-10-29): on by default.** `pool.sh run up-decay --seeds 1,2,3,4
--set tectonics.collision_upper_decay=true +DEEPTIME_CRUST_BUDGET=1
+DEEPTIME_CRUST_BUDGET_MAPS=@RUN@/maps` (key 05bc034a48ac, 8 runs), read against base30 (24) with the
default, `coastset`, `guard` and `collcoast` measures (medians, Mann-Whitney p). The collision
regime falls from 0.124 to 0.082 of the land and the coast within 150 km of a collision belt from
0.342 to 0.256: the interior's crust now lands near its front. The coast with high ground does not
move (v1census 0.155 against 0.157, p 0.88; version 1's rule 0.156 against 0.178, p 0.72): the
collision belts' own coasts are higher (their high-coast rate 0.384 to 0.464), since the crust the
interior no longer takes goes to the belt and the wedge, whose ends meet the sea. Land 0.333 (p
0.25), the largest landmass 0.169 (p 0.11), land above 2 km 0.047, collisions per 100 Myr 3.20
(p 0.15), criteria met 6 at the median and 6.25 in the mean against 5.79 (p 0.039). No guard step
beyond two Earth reliefs; the guard's worst cell 10,913 m from the sea against 10,152 (p 0.025),
the highest plate elevation 5,552 m (5,534). The physics is sourced and the pool clean, so it goes
on (the project's rule; the V1 numbers are not a gate). The high coasts are then the belts' own
ends, a question for the belt, not the interior.

### The collision window split (PLT-734 to PLT-736, 2026-10-30)

**Why.** One window, `collision_orogeny_myr` (30 Myr from a sample's last collision stamp,
PLT-079), served uses the sources time differently (PLT-079's note; design
docs/design/collision-window-split.md, PR #42 and its review): it made the collision regime, and
through the regime put the collision granites, the granite stocks and the thickened crust's
metamorphic burial in the first 30 Myr after each stamp, during the thrusting. Thermal models need
"at least 20 to 30 million yrs between collision and melting" (Hopkinson et al. 2017, p. 58), the
Himalaya's leucogranites came about 25 to 35 Myr after its collision (Weller et al. 2021), and
Thompson & England's (1984) Fig. 8 shows a 50 km thrust's melt field from 20 Myr after the thrust,
still there at 80 and gone by 120.

**What it does.** (1) A collision's stamp (`Sample::stamp_collision`) records the orogeny's onset
and its last collision stamp; an arc that later relabels the sample Andean (the 30 Myr guard)
leaves them, and a stamp more than `collision_melt_end_myr` after the last starts a new orogeny,
so hot crust thickened again goes on melting (PLT-734). The two times are packed into the 3 bytes
the `Sample` struct's alignment left free, the onset to the half-Myr and the last stamp to ±2 Myr,
since the full 16k preset's estimate fits its 5 GiB cap with about 1 MiB to spare. (2) The
collision regime is the active orogen: a Himalayan sample stamped this step or the last (PLT-734).
(3) The melt window, `tectonics.collision_melt_after_myr` 20 (PLT-735) to
`tectonics.collision_melt_end_myr` 80 (PLT-736), is written by the plates as the L1 layer
`plates/collision_melt`; the structure stage's collision granites (RCK-058), its granite stocks
(DEF-041, DEF-045: where they rise, the full rate, granite) and its metamorphic burial (RCK-032)
read it. (4) The lock and the Andean guard keep the 30 Myr.

**On the pool (arm win-split2, 2026-10-30): the default.** `pool.sh run win-split2 --seeds 1,2,3,4
+DEEPTIME_CRUST_BUDGET=1 +DEEPTIME_CRUST_BUDGET_MAPS=@RUN@/maps` (key b3e7ef433376, 8 runs), read
against base31's same seeds (arm base31-s4, cached) with the default, `guard`, `collcoast` and
`coastset` measures (medians, Mann-Whitney p). The planet changes, but within the seeds' spread:
the surface reads the regime below the collision regime in `finish_samples`' order (an arc's weak
lithosphere and load in the flexure, a trench in the advection), so a sample an arc or a trench
touches reads as one up to 30 Myr sooner, and the plates read the flexure back. Land 0.329 against
0.333 (p 0.72), largest landmass 0.165 against 0.169, continental crust under the sea 0.175
against 0.190, land above 2 km 0.043 against 0.047, coast with high ground 0.126 against 0.155
(p 0.96), land under ice 0.082 against 0.073, collisions per 100 Myr 2.35 against 3.20 (p 0.11),
criteria met median 6 (mean 6.00 against 6.25, p 0.50); the guard clean (no step beyond two Earth
reliefs, its worst 10,291 m against 10,913). The collision regime falls from 0.082 to 0.017 of the
land (`collcoast`), so the measures that read it move by definition: the coastset's collision
share of the high coasts 0.713 to 0.385 and the arc's 0.175 to 0.357. The structure stage's
counts, run for run against the same seeds (`summary.txt`): plutons emplaced × 1.29, pluton bodies
kept × 1.57, granite stocks × 1.59, dykes × 1.13 (the rifts the collision regime had hidden),
metamorphosed volume × 0.88, fold trains × 0.98, thrusts × 0.96. The melt window runs about
30 Myr longer than the old 30 Myr after the last stamp, and its plutons are younger, so more of
them survive erosion to the end.

**Where the collision high coasts are** (the lane's question, `collcoast`'s `geom_*` on the active
regime): 0.471 of them lie by a belt that runs along the coast, 0.287 where a belt runs out at the
coast, 0.270 by a belt that is not elongated; 0.721 are on landmasses of 0.10 of the land or more
(0.559 on base31-s4), and the collision land's median distance to the sea falls from 219 to 165 km
(p 0.028). What faces them (the crust-budget maps 50 Myr before each run's end, the 8 runs pooled;
a collision high coast within 150 km of a Himalayan sample stamped in the last 3 Myr): of the
1,596 by a belt along the coast, the nearest collision front is on the coast's own plate (0.764)
and a median 510 km away, and the sea in front is the coast's own plate's (0.729), mostly ocean
floor (0.728) a median 1,151 m deep; 0.056 of those seas lie at a front. They are the far coasts of
overriding blocks narrower than the belt's reach (PLT-241's 400 km and the interior's share), which
stack crust up to the block's own far coast; base31's same seeds read alike.

**Narrow upper plates on Earth** (read 2026-10-30, PLT-241's note). No source read gives the width
of the thickened belt on an upper plate or treats an upper plate narrower than the belt. Where the
upper plate is a narrow block, its back does rise: Taiwan's Coastal Range, the Luzon arc's crust,
stands 0 to 1.68 km (Lai et al. 2022). In the Banda arc "most of the shortening associated with
~70 km/Ma of plate convergence is taken up in other locations such as the back arc region (Wetar and
Flores Thrust systems), the rear of the accretionary wedge and at the deformation front in the Timor
Trough", and the Wetar Ridge overthrusts the South Banda Basin along the Wetar Thrust, "which takes
up some of the convergence" (Harris 2011): part of the convergence moves behind the block. And how an
indented continent thickens depends "mainly upon the degree of lateral confinement, but also upon
layer rheologies and the dimensions of indented and indenting continents" (Davy & Cobbold 1988). The
model has no back-arc thrust: the belt and the interior's share stack the crust up to the block's
far coast. A design for one is the lane's next lead (built: "A new subduction zone behind the
overriding block", below, PLT-737).

**Limits.** The melt window's end is the project's reading of one figure for one thrust, applied
from the last stamp of a belt thickened over many steps. The collision granites' rate per area
(RCK-058, 0.3 of the arc rate, a game choice) is unchanged, so their total grew with the window:
against Vigneresse & Burg 2003 (RCK-058's row) the rate already sat above Himalayan leucogranite
production.

### A new subduction zone behind the overriding block (PLT-737, 2026-10-30)

**Why.** The window split's arm showed the collision high coasts by a belt along the coast to be
the far coasts of overriding blocks narrower than the belt's reach (above): a collision against a
continent goes on stacking crust on the overriding plate until it stalls and welds (PLT-246) or its
incoming continent transfers (PLT-516), and the belt (PLT-241) and the interior's share (PLT-652,
over L = 2W/π, PLT-733) reach the block's far coast. Earth's narrow upper plates move part of the
convergence behind the block (Harris 2011, above). Ben chose to design and build that
(decisions log 2026-10-30, "Design, then build (Recommended)"; design docs/design/backarc-reversal.md).

**The process.** Stern 2004 (the library's full text, read again 2026-10-30) names two induced
nucleations after a collision: transference, and polarity reversal, which "also follows collision,
but continued convergence in this case results in a new subduction zone forming behind the
magmatic arc"; "the new subduction zone nucleates in the originally overriding plate". "The
geodynamics of INSZ polarity reversal for arcs have not been quantitatively modeled"; he expects
back-arc lithosphere to be "relatively thin and weak. Consequently, polarity reversal INSZ should
require less compression than transference INSZ". His example is the Solomon arc after the Ontong
Java Plateau, an oceanic arc, which PLT-371 already reverses at the contact; the new rule is for an
overriding plate with continental crust behind its front.

**The rule** (`tectonics.collision_backarc_reversal`, `collision::backarc_block`). In a collision
of a continent that has not stalled, whose slab is gone (the jam) and whose plates have converged by
100 km since (PLT-518), as for transference: the block is the overriding plate's visible
continental crust connected to its continental samples on the front; its back coast the block's
samples next to their own plate's ocean floor farther from the front than they are. The
collision's push reaches the back coast as the thin sheet's response does, by e^(−x/L) at the
distance x behind the front, L = 2W/π (PLT-733); when that push over the coast's length reaches
PLT-517's 3 × 10^12 N/m × g/g⊕, the block moves to the incoming plate (its groups get twins there,
the incoming plate carries its momentum, the crust that crossed the front stays under) and the
collision ends. The overriding plate keeps its ocean floor, which now meets the block's back coast,
where the force balance and the subduction rules decide what it does. Where transference is due
too, the margin with the larger force per metre ruptures. No new constant.

**The project's readings.** The decay on the overriding side and none on the incoming side follow
the model's own asymmetry: the overriding plate's interior deforms as a thin sheet (PLT-652,
PLT-733), the incoming continent is rigid, so transference's margin takes the whole push. The
threshold is transference's, though Stern expects less to suffice behind an arc: the conservative
choice, with no number to put in its place. x to the nearest front sample, and the tie-break.

**The unit test** (`a_narrow_overriding_block_moves_to_the_incoming_plate_behind_a_new_subduction_zone`,
`belts.rs`): on the two-plate fixture (a front 6,774 km long, L = 4,312 km), a strip 0.05 rad wide
behind the front passes 0.976 of the push to a back coast 7,319 km long; the whole half-continent
passes 0.656 to 10,176 km, so the push that just moves the strip leaves the half-continent in place.
It waits short of the force or the convergence and with the switch off; a stalled collision welds;
with transference on, the strip's force per metre (1.33 × 10^-7 per newton) beats the incoming
continent's margin (9.5 × 10^-8), so the block moves.

**Measured** (arm backarc, 8 runs, seeds 1 to 4 of both starts, key f3589be40bd8, against
base32-s4, base32's same seeds; `pool.sh table` with the default, `guard`, `collcoast` and
`coastset` measures). On by default from it (Ben's rule of 2026-10-23: the guard is clean).

| measure | base32-s4 | backarc | p |
|---|---|---|---|
| reversals behind the block a run | 0 | 16 to 23 (about 1.9 per 100 Myr) | |
| transferences a run | 15 to 30 | 6 to 15 | |
| collisions per 100 Myr | 2.35 | 3.90 | 0.021 |
| coast with high ground (≤ 0.11) | 0.126 | 0.114 | 0.23 |
| criteria met per run, median | 6 | 6.5 | 0.18 |
| continental crust under the sea | 0.175 | 0.267 | 0.065 |
| sea over the datum after 100 Myr / at the end, m | 449 / 430 | 541 / 687 | |
| largest landmass | 0.165 | 0.121 | 0.28 |
| land | 0.329 | 0.300 | 0.23 |
| the guard's worst, m from the sea | 10,291 | 10,518 | 0.33 |
| collision high coasts: the belt along the coast / ending at it | 0.471 / 0.287 | 0.493 / 0.281 | |
| high coasts: the collision belt's share / the arc's | 0.385 / 0.357 | 0.399 / 0.458 | |

Earth for the rate: Crameri et al. 2020 count 4 polarity reversals among 13 subduction initiations
since 104 Ma (PLT-056's row), on the whole planet; the model's 1.9 per 100 Myr are those behind a
continental block alone. The reversal now ends more continental collisions than transference does,
and collisions come more often because each ends sooner. What it costs: collisions that end sooner
stack less crust, so more continental crust stays near the normal column and floods (under the sea
0.267, the sea 687 m over the datum at the end). What it does not do: the collision high coasts by
a belt along the coast are as common a share as before, and the arc's share of the high coasts rose:
the block's back coast becomes the new subduction zone and grows an arc, so a high coast there is
now an arc's, as on Earth behind a reversal. The next lead for coast with high ground is not this
rule.

**What is left on base33, and the belt's width read again** (2026-10-30, PLT-241's second note).
On base33 (24 runs, the reversal on) the collision high coasts by a belt along the coast (the
crust-budget maps 50 Myr before each run's end, as above; a scratch script, not kept) number 3,722
against base32's 4,151; their nearest collision front lies a median 326 km away (528 km on base32),
on the coast's own plate for 0.725 of them, within 400 km for 0.564; the sea in front is their own
plate's (0.754); their high ground within 200 km stands a median 3,411 m over the sea (quartiles
2,889 and 3,939) on crust up to a median 61 km thick. The reversal took the far coasts of the
narrowest blocks; of what remains, 0.564 lies within the belt's reach (400 km) of its front. The sources on doubly
vergent orogens read again (PLT-241's second note) have the upper plate's wedge grow from the
singularity at the greater critical taper, and no fixed width from the onset; Taiwan's and Timor's
collision zones are 100 to 200 km wide. Taiwan's high ground near its east coast is the Central Range,
on the accreted Eurasian margin (the lower plate's crust); its upper plate, the Coastal Range (the
Luzon arc's crust), stands 0 to 1.68 km (Lai et al. 2022), well under these coasts' 3.4 km; the
Finisterre-Huon ranges, an accreting island arc terrane, stand 2 to 4 km at PNG's north coast. The model's default fill already widens
the belt from the front as it grows (PLT-600); 400 km bounds how far it spreads. A retro flank behind
fronts a median 326 km from these coasts would still stand high within 200 km of the coast, so no
rule follows from these sources alone that removes them. Taiwan's upper plate standing lower than
its orogen does suggest the default puts too much of the orogen on the overriding plate (the crust
that crosses the front is stacked on that plate's samples; the two wedges of PLT-730, which put the
pro-wedge on the incoming plate, are off): a lead, not a finding. The measure's own Earth figure (the M5 note,
docs/research/notes/m5-coast-high-ground-2026-10-25.md: Earth's coast within 200 km of a collision
boundary, 0.093 of the coast, is high for 0.135 of it) reads settings differently from `coastset`
(the model's collision belt coast, 0.084, high for 0.685), so the two are not compared here.

### The collision orogen (PLT-740, 2026-10-31)

The orogen lane, after Ben's order "Freeboard, then orogen (Recommended)" (decisions log 2026-10-30); the design
`docs/design/collision-orogen.md`. Measurement first, then one rule behind a switch. **Both switches,
`tectonics.collision_two_wedges` (PLT-730, PLT-731) and `tectonics.collision_retro_plateau` (PLT-740), are on by
default since 2026-10-31** (the coordinator's call under Ben's rule of 2026-10-23, "Always, fix V1 elsewhere";
decisions log 2026-10-31): sourced, unit-tested, the guard clean on the arm orog-cum, and the costs read below go to
the crust-budget lane.

- **The two wedges on the freeboard physics** (arm orog-tw-sedm, key 31c7c70bd7c7, argkey c7aa72cc: the two
  freeboard switches PLT-660 and PLT-661 set, as base34 has them on, and `tectonics.collision_two_wedges=true`;
  seeds 1 to 4 from both starts with the crust-budget environment, against the arm sedmargin, the same with the two
  wedges off; medians of 8, Mann-Whitney p in brackets). Land 0.238 to 0.214 (0.23), the largest landmass 0.097 to
  0.075 (0.028), continental crust under the sea 0.527 to 0.590 (0.13), land above 2 km 0.013 to 0.017 (0.96), coast
  with high ground 0.064 to 0.101 (0.23), the continental crust's net change +0.065 to +0.100 (0.010), criteria met
  6.5 to 5.5 (0.16), the sea at the end 169 to 221 m. The guard clean (worst 9,948 m from the sea against 9,964, no
  step beyond two Earth reliefs), the highest plate elevation 4,288 to 4,476 m (0.72). The incoming plate's wedge
  holds 0.545 of the kept crust (0.054 with the taper belt; `tools/review/orogen/dock.py` on the globals), the
  interior's share 0.072 to 0.051: about Wolf et al. 2021's partition of the shortening, 60 % on the pro side once
  the retro-wedge shortens (p. 13). The colliding margins are still drowned with the freeboard on: the incoming crust
  at the front above the sea, front-time weighted over collision states under 30 Myr, is 0.586 on base33 and 0.320 on
  sedmargin (PLT-661 makes the distal margins continental crust under the sea, and they collide first); with the two
  wedges 0.543 (the pro-wedge raises it before it reaches the front). `collcoast`: the collision regime's land within
  150 km of the sea 0.591 to 0.656, its median distance to the sea 121 to 104 km (0.19). `coastset`: the rifted
  margins' share of the high coasts 0.042 to 0.122 (the pro-wedge on the incoming plate's rifted margin). On the
  census grid (`tools/review/m5diag`, against SRTM15+): M5 0.067 to 0.099 (Earth 0.084), M4 0.013 to 0.017 (0.055),
  the high ground near the coast 0.49 to 0.52 (0.115). So the mechanism works on dry and drowned margins alike, and it
  does not rebuild the mountains: for the same cross-section the two wedges' crest stands at sqrt(1 / (1 + tan α /
  tan β)), 0.78, of the one-sided belt's (the lane's arithmetic), and the pro-wedge fills drowned margins first.
- **Where the high ground goes** (`tools/review/orogen/hiseries.py`: every 50 Myr crust-budget map after the first
  100 Myr). The land above 2 km, mean over a run's maps (median of the runs), is 0.048 on base33 (24 runs), 0.027 on
  sedmargin, 0.022 with the two wedges; the land above 4 km 0.0050, 0.0020 and 0.0008, at its largest 0.022, 0.010 and
  0.0056. Tibet-class ground forms in large collisions and does not last: on sedmargin's supercontinent-1 a collision
  from −166 to −104 Myr (front 5,529 km, shortening 5,848 km) left 0.065 of the land above 2 km at −100 Myr, 724
  samples (about 3.6 million km²) above 4 km on crust 65 to 68 km thick, and 0.011 at the end
  (`tools/review/orogen/orostats.py`). On two runs of each arm (`erosion_bands`), flat high ground (above 2 km,
  relief under 500 m) loses 109 to 129 m/Myr of rock, steep high ground 465 to 509 m/Myr, though the flat high
  ground is arid or polar by its Köppen class (`tools/review/orogen/hiclimate.py`, the final fields: arid 0.475 on
  base33 and 0.567 on sedmargin, polar 0.428 and 0.268); the Altiplano-Puna's internally drained interior erodes at
  0.02 ± 0.0004 mm/yr (one sample, Bookhagen & Strecker 2012, pp. 103-104), southern Tibet's under 0.01 km/Myr
  (ERO-174). The plateau's wear, not the orogen's placement, is what keeps a Tibet-class plateau from lasting to a
  run's end (STATUS Follow-ups, "High plateaus still wear too fast").
- **The rule** (PLT-740, `tectonics.collision_retro_plateau`, on by default since 2026-10-31; with
  `collision_two_wedges` only). Past the
  strength height the two wedges' plateau grows retro-ward through the overriding plate's continental crust as far
  as the step's crust needs, not to `collision_belt_km` only: when the fill leaves crust with the retro flank's
  samples within the belt's reach at their limits, the flank is searched again through that plate's continental
  samples (twice the reach each time) and the same fill runs over it, until the crust is placed or the connected crust
  is all taken. Vanderhaeghe et al. 2003 (full text): the orogen stays back-to-back wedges until the base of the
  thickened crust weakens, then "the plateaux grow laterally at constant thickness between characteristic edge peaks"
  (p. 27), "it is the net retro-ward flow that accounts for retro-ward growth of the plateau" (p. 41), and the
  plateau's crustal thickness "is determined mainly by the properties of the cold crust" of the flanking wedges
  (pp. 28-29), which the strength height (PLT-253) stands for. Wolf et al. 2021 (p. 25): a large hot plateau forms
  "located mostly on the retro-side". Medvedev & Beaumont (preprint, p. 3): "plateaus grow outward by tectonic
  thickening and accretion of adjacent crust in the transition zone". Before it, what the belt's reach could not hold
  went to the no-room rule (PLT-700), stacked above the strength height by the belt's profile, nearest the front, and
  moved on by the step's ceiling and the surface's channel flow; on the two-wedge arm that was 0.010 of the kept
  crust, so the rule changes where little crust lands, and only in large collisions.
- **Structures on the plateau** (2026-10-31, after PR #50's review). The plateau's samples are stamped as the
  collision's orogeny (the regime, the provinces, the young-orogen weakness) but stay outside the collision's footprint
  (PLT-260: no convergence, shortening or carrier), so the structure stage gives them no collision folds or thrusts.
  Their crust comes by the orogen's flow from the front, not by shortening their own upper crust: Tibet's eastern margin
  was "uplifted without significant shortening of the upper crust along large-magnitude thrust faults" and its
  thickening is "mainly in the deep crust" (Clark & Royden 2000, p. 703, full text), with "little crustal shortening"
  there since about 4 Ma (Royden et al. 1997, abstract); the interior extends east-west (Armijo et al. 1986, abstract:
  normal faulting "the dominant tectonic regime north of the Himalayas in the last 2 ± 0.5 m.y.", extension N96°E;
  Blisniuk et al. 2001, abstract: graben in central Tibet since at least 13.5 Myr). Against it, Vanderhaeghe et al.
  2003 find one model's plateau velocity field "indicates pure shear thickening in the upper crust" (p. 40), beside
  "low deformation rates in the upper crust during the later, plateau stage" (p. 42). Not modelled: the interior's
  normal faults and rifts, and Clark & Royden's southern margin, "where crustal thickening can be explained by
  shortening of the upper crust through faulting and folding" (p. 703), which the belt within its reach stands for.
- **What limits the overriding plate's share** (no new rule). While the crest is under the strength height the
  retro-wedge at the greater taper holds tan α / (tan α + tan β) of an even-ground cross-section, 0.39; a narrow
  overriding block holds what its retro flank reaches before its far coast, which stands at H − w tan β for a block w
  wide (Taiwan's belt is the lower plate's margin, its arc the backstop: Dahlen 1990, pp. 83-84; Simoes et al. 2007,
  p. 1); past the strength height every new step's crust goes to the retro plateau, as Tibet holds most of its
  orogen's crust on the upper plate; and the interior's thin-sheet share (PLT-652, PLT-733).
- **The cumulative arm** (orog-cum, the branch `collision-orogen` on master f80d75a8, key f2d6412d801f, argkey
  d3261b0a: `--set tectonics.collision_two_wedges=true --set tectonics.collision_retro_plateau=true`, seeds 1 to 4
  from both starts, the crust-budget environment) against base34-s4 (the freeboard merge's seeds 1 to 4; sedmargin's
  runs bit for bit) and base34 (24 runs), medians, p in brackets against base34-s4 and then base34. Land 0.238 to
  0.205 (0.13; base34 0.227, 0.057), the largest landmass 0.097 to 0.074 (0.16), continental crust under the sea 0.527
  to 0.605 (0.23; base34 0.540, 0.046: over the check's 0.56), land above 2 km 0.013 to 0.013 (0.72; base34 0.022,
  0.22), coast with high ground 0.064 to 0.067 (0.96; base34 0.078, 0.48), the continental crust's net change +0.065
  to +0.094 (0.083; base34 +0.063, 0.013), criteria met 6.5 to 6, the sea at the end 169 to 203 m. The guard clean
  (worst 9,945 m, no step beyond two Earth reliefs, the highest plate elevation 4,162 m). The plateau rule placed a
  median 0.0005 of the kept crust beyond the belt's reach (0.0037 at most; `dock.py`), the no-room rule 0.0087; the
  pro-wedge 0.533, the interior 0.052. `collcoast`: the collision regime 0.023 to 0.013 of the land, 0.729 of it within
  150 km of the sea, belts not elongated 0.196 to 0.075 (0.001). `coastset`: the collision belt's rate on its own coast
  0.564 to 0.353, the rifted margins' share of the high coasts 0.042 to 0.125. The census grid: M5 0.092, M4 0.013, the
  coast within 200 km of a collision high for 0.37 of it (base34-s4 0.48, Earth 0.135). The high ground through time
  (`hiseries.py`): above 2 km 0.030 on base34 (24 runs) to 0.024, above 4 km 0.0023 to 0.0012.
  Since the plateau rule moved under a thousandth of the crust, orog-cum and orog-tw-sedm are the same physics but for
  that, and their differences are the seeds' chaos re-rolled: coast with high ground 0.101 against 0.067, the
  collision belt's rate on its coast 0.539 against 0.353. That is the noise floor of an 8-run arm for these measures.
  What both arms show alike: the largest landmass down (0.075 and 0.074), continental crust under the sea up (0.590
  and 0.605), the crust's net change up (+0.100 and +0.094, p 0.001 and 0.013 against base34), the high ground through
  time down (above 2 km 0.022 and 0.024 against 0.030, above 4 km 0.0008 and 0.0012 against 0.0023). The two wedges

  where it thickens crust that stays under the sea, and their crest stands lower; the coast with high ground is not
  resolved either way.
- **Tests.** `the_retro_plateau_grows_past_the_belt_through_its_own_crust`: a head-on collision whose pro side and
  retro flank within the belt's reach stand at the strength height, and whose overriding lowland stands 20 m under it
  for 400 km up to a 400 km strip of ocean floor (so that one step's crust reaches the ocean; on 300 m lowland it fills
  about 120 km); with the switch every sample of that lowland rises, at most to the strength height, nothing on the
  ocean floor or across it does, the no-room rule (PLT-700) takes the rest, more than none and less than without the
  switch, and the crust kept is the same as without it, to 1e-6; off, nothing beyond the belt rises. The plateau
  grows through continental crust under the sea too; it stops at ocean floor. `an_arc_in_collision_takes_the_crust_on_its_edge_on_the_shipped_path`:
  the shipped switches (two wedges, the plateau, PLT-700) on an arc in collision whose incoming continent already
  stands at the strength height; no plateau, and the no-room rule puts the step's crust on the arc's edge at the
  front, all of it kept.

## How small terranes dock (PLT-770, PLT-771, 2026-10-30)

The coast-with-high-ground audit (docs/research/notes/coast-high-ground-audit-2026-10-30.md) read
the model's small terranes as turned into collision belts: terranes under 50 samples are 0.54 of the
hand-offs, they dock in 0 to 2 Myr, and 0.95 of the crust that crosses their fronts stays as thickness
on the overriding plate (PLT-242), where "on Earth such fragments accrete as area or subduct". The
docking lane measured base33's cached runs, read the sources and built the missing branch behind a
switch, `tectonics.terrane_docking_cover` (on by default since 2026-10-31, decisions log). Design: docs/design/small-terrane-docking.md (its
tables in full).

### What base33 does with them (24 runs, measurement only)

`tools/review/terranes/dock_records.py` (the dynamics record, the crust budget) and
`tools/review/terranes/dock_maps.py` (the crust-budget maps), on key 31c7c70bd7c7:

- **How many and how fast.** Hand-offs of terranes under 50 samples (about 255,000 km², a sample
  5,100 km²) come 29.2 times per 100 Myr, 50 to 200 samples 13.3, 200 to 1,000 samples 8.6, larger 3.9
  (medians over the runs); partings 15.0 parted, 4.3 reversed, 4.9 closed, 1.2 open at the end. Under 50 samples a hand-off lasts 0 / 0 / 4 Myr (p25 / p50 / p75) with 123 / 151 /
  200 km of shortening, all on PLT-068's threshold, at a convergence that does not slow (54.8 mm/yr at
  the onset, 60.1 at the end): half dock in the step they begin, one step's convergence crossing.
- **How much each crossing keeps.** 30,200 / 42,500 / 62,400 km² of crust crosses, 0.086 of all the
  crust crossing collision fronts by area; at the run's mean crossing thickness (32.8 km) and kept
  share (0.946), 0.94 / 1.31 / 1.93 million km³ a hand-off. Of what reached the front, 0.35 (the median;
  0.52 pooled) crossed and the rest moved to the overriding plate as area.
- **How high their belts stand.** The front's largest uplift, summed over the steps, is 3.5 / 5.1 /
  7.6 km; at the run's end the land those hand-offs stamped (0.046 of the land) stands 219 / 498 / 702
  m over the sea (p90 1,244 m), 0.056 of it above 2 km, a median 374 km from the sea.
- **How much of the coast with high ground they make.** On the final map (the plate model's ground on
  100,000 Fibonacci points, M5 0.142 against the census grid's 0.1325; each collision stamp matched to
  its collision state by plate and time, 0.66 of the points with more than one candidate), the
  nearest qualifying high ground of 0.0099 of the coast is a hand-off under 50 samples', 0.0037 one of
  50 to 200; without those two classes' high ground M5 is 0.1288, 0.0055 lower (0.0082 by the mean
  over runs). The collisions open at the end hold 0.0547 (without them M5 is 0.095), the Andean
  margins 0.0284.
- **What they are.** The bodies of one plate's continental crust under 50 samples, not their plate's
  largest (127 a snapshot from -900 to -50 Myr), have 19.0 km of own crust at the median (8.9 to 34.2
  from p10 to p90), 0.73 of them island arcs by their magma (14.4 km on 7 km of ocean crust), the
  rest 28.6 km; 0.18 of them dry.
- **How big they are across the front.** The hand-offs under 50 samples reach 333 / 455 / 642 km
  across the front (the shortening plus the rest's area over the front's length; p10 254, p90 887);
  the larger classes 1,236 km and more at the median.

### What Earth does

A Sonnet research sub-agent read the sources (copied in the design with pages; the full texts of
Cloos 1993 and Tetreault & Buiter 2012 could not be got, their abstracts were read). Small buoyant
bodies go down with the slab, scraped of a sliver: "the force of the subducting slab drives
subduction and can most likely overcome the buoyancy of small crustal units (Molnar and Gray, 1979;
Cloos, 1993)", "Seamounts and submarine volcanics subduct easily if they are not incorporated into the
accretionary prism" (Tetreault & Buiter 2014, p. 1265); "in most cases only the upper 2–5 km of arc
crust are accreted onto continents through thin-skinned thrusting and preserved. This most likely
occurs when island arcs are on the subducting plate" (p. 1251); seamounts "generally subducted, with
only thin slices of basalts (<1 km thick) being offscraped" (Clift et al. 2009, p. 95); "lithospheric
buoyancy does not prevent FAT subduction during constant convergence" (Tetreault & Buiter 2012,
abstract). Larger ones jam and dock: "Many of the larger FATs such as oceanic plateaus and continental
fragments are accreted by collision" (Tetreault & Buiter 2014, p. 1246), underplating "perhaps the
most common type of terrane accretion" (p. 1245), "terrane–continent collision leaving behind accreted
terranes 25–40 km thick" (p. 1243). The size between: Yan et al. 2021 (abstract) find steep subduction
"without subduction zone reorganization" for a "small‐sized (≤150 km)" plateau and a breakoff and flat
slab, or a jump behind the plateau, for a "moderate‐sized (≥300 km)" one with a depleted root. The
upper plate over a docking body: the Cordillera de Talamanca over the subducting Cocos Ridge, "rock
uplift ... no greater than ∼2 km" and "40 km since the Pliocene" of shortening (Morell et al. 2012);
the Yakutat terrane's "Earth’s highest coastal mountain range" (Enkelmann et al. 2008); Taiwan's
accreting Luzon arc 0 to 1.68 km (Lai et al. 2022).

### Reading the model against them

At the quick planet's 71-km lattice the model's "small" terranes are moderate bodies: 333 to 642 km
across the front (p25 to p75), Yan et al.'s reorganizing size, island arcs at Cloos's 15 km and
continental fragments near Tetreault & Buiter's 24.8 km mean. Docking them as collisions is in kind
Earth's (the rest of the terrane accretes as area, the crossing underplates the overriding plate's
edge), and the land they leave stands at Talamanca's and the Coastal Range's heights. They hold about
0.006 to 0.008 of M5 at most (the audit's +0.01 about), and that part is not missing physics. What is
missing is the small branch: a body the slab can pull down is docked as a collision too.

### The law (`tectonics.terrane_docking_cover`, PLT-770, PLT-771; on by default since 2026-10-31)

Each step, at each collision front whose contact still has a slab of the pair: the slab's reach
against a body's buoyancy, S* = L / (1 + 2.25 T / 30 km) (FRC-030's buoyancy of the dragged length
against the pull of the dense slab left; L the slab's length up to 700 km, PLT-184; T the body's crust
thickness at the front): 215 km under 30 km of crust, 329 km under 15 km. Each body at the front is
judged on its own, its extent across the front being all its area (the part already under the
overriding plate and the rest) over its share of the front's length; the front goes down when every
body is within its S*, a body beyond holding the whole front, and keeps that judgment while its
bodies go down (each body remembered by its samples; one that crust joins is judged again, alone,
by all its samples over the share of the front it was judged with). Then of the crossing crust only the cover
(sediment, sedimentary and volcanic rock, PLT-771: 2.5 km of a model island arc of 15 km, inside the
"upper 2–5 km") and the crust this collision stacked on it stay, pool by pool, by PLT-242's share, all
of it on the overriding plate (no pro-wedge on a terrane going down: the cover is offscraped against
the overriding plate, "added onto the accretionary prism"); the rest is counted as
`plates/collision_stripped_km3`; it does not transfer at PLT-068's threshold, and its front feeds the
slab instead of blocking it (FRC-019). A larger terrane jams and collides as before. The extent
condition is the project's reading of Cloos's buoyancy for a body of finite size along the slab
(Cloos's own result is a thickness). It is not bracketed by Yan et al.: it takes in their 150 km at any
thickness but passes their 300 km under crust thinner than about 18 km, where they find the slab
breaks off and subducts flat or the subduction jumps (the model has neither); nor is it conservative
either way (it leaves out the help of the slab beside a body short along the trench, and takes the
slab's whole pull with no resistance of the mantle). The pull is not applied at the terrane's own
front samples (continental front samples resist only): it goes down at the convergence the plates'
other forces keep.

On base33 the hand-offs within that reach are 0.054 (220 km, continental fragments) to 0.127 (270 km,
arcs) of those under 50 samples and almost none of the larger, so the law is expected to move the
coast with high ground by less than the small terranes' 0.006 to 0.008 and the continental crust by a
few hundredths of a km³ a year (the project's estimates before the arm). On base34 (the freeboard
merge) the small bodies are fewer and thinner (60 a snapshot against 127, a median 10 km of own crust
against 19, 0.75 of their samples under Cloos's 15 km), so the reach is longer (308 km under 17 km of
crust, 391 km under 10.5 km, on a full slab) and 0.18 to 0.38 of the hand-offs under 50 samples are
within it, while their share of the coast with high ground fell to 0.002 to 0.004: the expected move is
less than that, and about 0.02 to 0.07 km³ a year of crust (the project's estimates). A finer lattice
resolves smaller bodies, and there it reaches more of them.

On the pool (2026-10-31; arm small-terrane, key dcf0d7480ef3, 8 runs, on the collision orogen's
physics, PLT-730, PLT-731 and PLT-740 set on, against orog-cum, the same physics without the law;
medians, Mann-Whitney p in brackets): the guard clean (the worst 10,154 m from the sea against 9,945,
p 0.51; no step beyond 2 Earth reliefs). Hand-offs under 50 samples 12.3 per 100 Myr against 17.6
(p 0.014), the larger classes unchanged; partings 29.2 against 23.3, 5.8 per 100 Myr of them terranes
that went down whole; crust stripped 0.035 km³ a year (p25 to p75 0.029 to 0.043), about 1 % of Stern &
Scholl's 3.2 km³ a year of additions. No V1 number beyond the seeds' spread: land 0.222 against 0.205
(p 0.19), the largest landmass 0.083 against 0.074 (p 0.33), continental crust under the sea 0.567
against 0.605 (p 0.16), the coast with high ground 0.091 against 0.067 (p 0.38); collision high coasts on
landmasses under 0.02 of the land 0.359 against 0.668 (p 0.44). The design's "What the arm showed" has
the rest. That arm ran the first build, which PR #51's review (2026-10-31) corrected: the two wedges put
the kept cover on the terrane going down (its pro flank), where it crossed again and was stripped;
the restacked rock took the cover's mix; two bodies at one front were pooled; the slab broke off
under a body slower than 10 Myr; and the extent, read each step as the shortening plus the visible
rest, overshot halfway down by the lattice's lag. The build above is the corrected one.

Its arm (small-terrane-2, key a7bb6d240ebe, the same settings and seeds, against orog-cum; master's
heat flow of late continental crust, PLT-469, is in it too): hand-offs under 50 samples 13.3 per 100
Myr against 17.6 (p 0.010), partings 30.4 against 23.3 (p 0.005), collision high coasts on landmasses
under 0.02 of the land 0.346 against 0.668 (p 0.038), crust stripped 0.033 km³ a year; no step beyond
2 Earth reliefs, the deepest trench floor 10,243 m against 9,945 (p 0.001), half the guard's 19.8 km;
no V1 number beyond the seeds' spread (the coast with high ground 0.092 against 0.067, p 0.33; land
0.210 against 0.205, p 0.80; continental crust under the sea 0.582 against 0.605, p 1.0).

## Sediment by margin type and the margin's sediment (PLT-660 to PLT-662, 2026-10-25)

The drowning diagnosis (build log 2026-10-25, "M5 lane: why the land drowns on m5-unfreeze") found the
sea standing about 700 m over the datum because oceanic-labelled crust of 15 km and more takes the
basins' volume. That crust is built mostly from the continents' sediment, on ocean floor next to the
continents that never recycles. On base15's seeds 1 to 4 it is 0.269 of the oceanic samples at the
end (m5thickoc), and refilling the oceanic crust of 10 km and more as a normal ocean column lowers the
counterfactual sea by about 1,000 m (m5sea). Earth keeps that rock out of the ocean basins two ways:
the margin's own sediment lies on thinned continental crust, and a trench sends most of what reaches it
down. Two stages were asked for, each behind its own switch, with tests written first:

- (a) margin material within Brune et al. 2014's 70 to 200 km stays continental, the width taken from
  the source, and the spread path labelled by its rock;
- (b) PLT-440's flat 0.12 replaced by Clift & Vannucchi 2004's share by the margin's type.

### The rules

- **(b) Sediment subduction by the margin's type** (PLT-660, `tectonics.sediment_subduction_sourced`).
  At a resampling the slab takes 0.83 of the sediment and sedimentary pools of the floor that went
  under where the pile is thicker than 1 km and the convergence is slower than 76 mm/yr, and all of
  it otherwise. Clift & Vannucchi 2004: accretion works "when convergent rates are <76 mm yr-1 and
  where the sedimentary cover is >1 km thick", and "Even at the accretionary margins, typically 83% of
  the incoming sedimentary pile is subducted". von Huene & Scholl 1991: at erosive margins
  "effectively all incoming sediment is subducted". The rule holds whatever the top's crust, so an
  intra-oceanic margin's thin pile (the Mariana, Tonga) goes down whole, where PLT-440 accreted 88 %
  of it to the top.
- **(a) The margin's sediment is continental** (PLT-661, `tectonics.margin_sediment_continental`).
  The rifted-margin taper's ocean side (PLT-261, −W/2 < d < 0, the crust thinning from 20 to 7 km) is
  where Earth's margins have their necking and hyper-extended domains: continental crust thinned to
  under 10 km, "slivers that vary in widths between 70 km offshore Iberia and 200 km off Angola"
  (Brune et al. 2014). A member there that is ocean floor and holds rock from the continents
  (sediment and sedimentary rock beyond the open ocean's pile for its age and latitude) turns
  continental at the end of the step, over its own ocean crust as its basement (PLT-331). Members with
  the rain alone, at a trench, in a subduction zone or on an arc stay oceanic. The line was the
  plates' pelagic rain, 5 m/Myr times the age (PLT-103); since that was retired (the pelagic lane,
  2026-10-25) the surface stage lays the rain, and the line is GlobSed's eq. 2a less its pore water
  (`surface::pelagic::open_floor_solid_m`, ERO-215; erosion-and-sediment.md "The pelagic rain"),
  which the rain lies 14 to 42 m in place under.
- **The side rule.** So that a converted member is never the next member's margin, the taper takes a
  continental column with under 10 km of its own crystalline crust (`hyper_extended`) as its ocean
  side, not its continental side, and ocean crust the taper adds to it joins its basement. A matured
  island arc (8 km of its own over its basement) falls under the same test, so with the switch on it
  is the ocean side too. The zone is found as the step begins, so a step's conversions do not move it
  within the step.
- **The spread's rock** (PLT-662, the same switch). The collapse, the founder and a rate release fill
  ocean floor up to the normal column before it turns continental (PLT-277), so up to 32 km of
  continental rock stood under the oceanic label. With the switch on the receiver turns continental at
  once when the rock is continental (always for the collapse and the founder, and for a rate release
  when continental columns gave more than half of it). This is a bookkeeping rule (`game-choice`).

No value was chosen: 1 km, 76 mm/yr, 0.83 and 10 km are read in the sources, and W is PLT-262's 200
km. On the quick planet's 68 to 71 km spacing, W/2 reaches ring 1 only. Unit tests (written first):
`sediment_goes_down_by_the_margins_type` and `a_resampling_subducts_sediment_by_the_margins_type` for
(b); `the_margins_sediment_turns_its_distal_margin_continental` (every member with 2,500 m of pile in
the zone turns, none with the rain alone, none on the subducting plate, and over 30 steps the crust
and heights equal the switch-off run's) and `spread_continental_rock_is_continental_at_once_with_the_margin_switch`
for (a). deeptime-core's tests pass (1,079).

One deviation from the source, on the first arm: PLT-660 read the top sample's `convergence_mm_yr`,
which subduction.rs stamps as the plates' whole relative speed at the front (the normal component
only with `DEEPTIME_ARC_NORMAL=1`). Clift & Vannucchi's 76 mm/yr is an orthogonal rate, so an oblique
margin read faster and its pile went down whole where the normal component alone would accrete 17 %
of it. Fixed for the second arm ("The blend closed (PLT-663)" below): the front stamps the normal
component as its own field and PLT-660 reads it.

### Where the stock lies (the ring split, before the arm)

The diagnostic run (base15's supercontinent-1 with the pools maps, key fb136aadfe68, argkey cd665cef;
its world matches base15's run) split the oceanic-labelled stock beyond the 7 km ocean column with
m5pools.py. The stock is 3,216 m planet-mean, of it 1,494 m of the continents' sediment. By
distance to the plate's own continent, in sample spacings, it lies:

| ring 1 | ring 2 | ring 3 | ring 4 and beyond | on plates with no continent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.46 | 0.19 | 0.11 | 0.18 | 0.06 |

So (a) at Brune's taper can reach under half of it. The rest is sediment on ocean floor farther out,
Earth's continental rise and abyssal fans, which lie on oceanic crust on Earth too and stay oceanic.
On that run, m5margins.py's converted-margin reading (continental crust over a basement with under
10 km of its own, no arc magma) finds 0.0001 of the planet with no relabel: that is the reading's
floor, and the share with and without the converted margins is the same there (0.401, 0.401).

earthlike_quick_16k, 1,000 Myr, 2 threads), `--set tectonics.sediment_subduction_sourced=true
tectonics.margin_sediment_continental=true` and the crust budget's two envs. The base is base15's seeds
1 to 4 (e5e78994377c, cd665cef, `@4`, the same envs). Both stages run together, as one cumulative arm.

The guard stays clean. Its worst is 9,831 m against 10,251 (p 0.10). No step goes beyond two Earth

M4 (m4table, p50) falls from 0.0261 to 0.0026: young belts 0.0131 to 0.0015 of the land, arcs and

What the stages were meant to fix moved as intended. The thick oceanic-labelled crust (m5thickoc,
